FOLLOW-UPS FILED: gort-k1z (the guide also subscribes to the NEXT block, which after 18:00 is tomorrow's, and this transmitter carries one day); gort-qxl.1 noted, because the ALL CHANNELS grid was last measured when only one block was ever on air. The startup warning about non-drawing days and the config caveat are removed rather than reworded -- any date and any hour now draw.

title: [TASK-5.13] Fit the box and the whole handset on screen at once
description:
gort-4sx.26 pinned the screen so it stays in view while you scroll. That was the smaller half of the problem and the user said so plainly: the REMOTE still scrolls, so the sky key and the number pad are never on screen together and the handset is awkward to use. The goal is no page scrolling at all on a desktop window -- screen and whole handset side by side, both fully visible.

Measured budget at 1440x900: header 54, grid padding-top 48, so 798px of usable height. The controls column is 849 (heading 53 + remote 719 + feedback 38) and the viewer column is 1102 (intro 264 + television 652 + status 62 + actions 44 + margins). Two independent things therefore have to give, and neither alone is enough:

1. The intro is 264px inside the LEFT COLUMN, so every pixel it takes comes off the television. Moved out to span both columns and compacted, the viewer column becomes television + status + actions and the picture keeps its natural size.
2. The remote is 719 against a 798 budget that also has to hold the heading and the feedback line. Its key ROWS are only ~498 of that; the rest is padding, gaps and margins. Those get viewport-height clamps so the handset compresses as the window shortens. Key targets stay at 44px minimum -- the existing a11y test asserts it and a transform:scale() would shrink the hit areas below the floor, so scaling the remote is the wrong mechanism.

Floor: roughly 616px of content, so no scrolling down to about a 720px window. Below that the page scrolls as it does now and the pinned stage from gort-4sx.26 carries it.

spec: plan/phase-5-browser-and-deploy.md
-> /go-engineer
[TC-5.15]
close_reason:
The desktop page now IS the window: at 1366x768, 1440x900 and 1920x1080 nothing scrolls and the screen, status, reset and the whole handset from the sky key to the 0 key are all visible, with every key still at its 44px floor. Measured zero overflow at every window >=760px tall; below that the page scrolls with the picture pinned, which is honest -- two columns of 44px keys do not fit beside a picture in 620px of height.

Three mechanisms, two discarded, and the CSS records why so nobody retries them: (1) a constant subtracted from 100vh assumes everything that is not the picture has a fixed height, which is false because the standing copy appears on tall windows and the handset compresses on short ones -- one swept value fitted 1440x900 exactly and overflowed every other size, giving a 138px picture at 1280x620; (2) width: fit-content could not shrink the bezel to the picture, because a canvas contributes its INTRINSIC 720px as max-content width whatever height it is drawn at, so the image stayed centred in a full-width bezel. What works: a bounded height (height, not min-height -- percentage heights inside only resolve against a definite one), the handset compressing through spacing only, and the set sized from the stage's own height with container-query units, so there is no constant to re-sweep when copy changes.

Also found by measuring rather than reasoning: .site-shell's 48px bottom padding was the entire 34px overflow at 1366x768, and the controls heading cost 62px the remote could not give up, so it is visually hidden there while staying in the accessibility tree -- the column is named by it through aria-labelledby.

TC-5.15 asserts all three fitted sizes plus the short-window fallback, falsified by deleting the fit block (all three fail). 21/21 Playwright, CSS lint clean, light and dark inspected at 1366x768, mobile re-verified unchanged at 390x780.

title: Remove the per-instruction heap allocation in board.StepWithHooks
description:
The emulator heap-allocates once per emulated instruction. board.StepWithHooks takes StepHooks by value and stores r.hooks = &hooks, which makes the parameter escape -- 'go build -gcflags=-m' reports 'internal/board/runtime.go:192:33: moved to heap: hooks' -- and Step() calls it for every instruction. The CPU profile attributes 14.31% cumulative to mallocgc reached ONLY from StepWithHooks, with another ~6% in the defer machinery that clears the field.

Approach to evaluate, not a decided design: keep the hooks as a value field rather than a pointer, or give Step a path that does not go through the hooks wrapper at all, and drop the per-instruction defer. The StepHooks mechanism exists so diagnostic tools observe the same ordered loop without building a second board (runtime.go), so whatever replaces it must keep that property -- a second stepping path that instruments differently is the thing the current design was written to avoid.

Acceptance is a MEASUREMENT, not an inspection: the bare restored-snapshot step loop is 191.6 ns/instruction today, and the change must move that number with the oracle gate and the boot gate still passing. Bank the benchmark so the next regression is visible; there is no throughput gate in CI today, which is how this went unnoticed.

Expect roughly 20M instr/s if the whole wrapper overhead goes, not spike 001's 44.2M: the CPU core is about a quarter of the profile. See gort-4sx.24's notes for the full measurement trail.
-> /go-engineer
[no-test: a benchmark and the existing boot and oracle gates are the check]
close_reason:
board.StepWithHooks stored the address of its by-value StepHooks parameter, which moved it to the heap -- 'go build -gcflags=-m' reported 'internal/board/runtime.go:192:33: moved to heap: hooks' -- and Step calls it once per emulated instruction. The machine therefore allocated once per instruction and paid for the defer that cleared the field. The field now holds the hooks BY VALUE and the defer is gone.

MEASURED, not inspected. Bare restored-snapshot step loop: 206.0 ns/instruction with 1 alloc/op and 51 B/op, down to 94.75 ns/instruction with 0 allocs/op -- 2.17x, and more than the CPU profile's flat attribution predicted, because 51 bytes an instruction was also feeding the collector. End to end in the real server loop, same measurement that produced the original figure: 3.2M -> 6.90M instructions/sec, 2.16x.

The defer was removable because the invariant is structural, not defended: r.hooks is read only by the clock pump, the clock is advanced only from inside StepWithHooks, and every entry assigns the field first -- Step passes an empty StepHooks. I wrote TestStaleHooksNeverFire to guard the window and then DELETED it, because it passed just as happily against a pointer field with no defer, which is the exact bug it claimed to catch: the state is unreachable, and a test for an unreachable branch is coverage-shaped nothing. The reasoning is in the code instead.

Banked so it cannot drift back: internal/board/step_bench_test.go carries BenchmarkStep with both readings recorded, and TestStepDoesNotAllocate, which asserts the property the number came from. That test FAILED before the change (1.0 allocs per instruction) and passes after -- watched failing, not assumed.

ACCEPTANCE: go test -race ./... clean, ctl.sh lint 0 issues, boot gate ok, and the ORACLE GATE AGREES over 470,000 checkpoints through 469,999,000 instructions with 42 guest tasks -- behaviour is bit-identical to the browser oracle after the change, which is the check that matters for touching the instruction loop.

NOT CLOSED AS 'NFR MET'. 94.75 ns is ~10.6M instructions/sec against a 15M/s NFR. The allocation defect is gone; the gap is not. The remaining time is spread across the CPU core (~45% of the in-loop profile), the bus and the icount clock, with no single defect of this kind left. Anyone reading the new profile should note that its memmove and sha256 samples are the benchmark's own firmware load and snapshot restore -- b.ResetTimer does not reset the CPU profiler -- and not the loop.

title: [TASK-5.12] Keep the screen in line with the handset while scrolling
description:
On a desktop viewport shorter than the page, scrolling down to reach the lower handset keys takes the television off the top of the screen, so the viewer cannot watch the box and press its keys at the same time. Measured 2026-09-20 at 1280x620: scrolled to the bottom, the canvas is 56 percent visible (top at -265) while the number pad sits at -16. The narrow breakpoints already solve this -- .television is position:sticky below 760px -- but the desktop layout leaves it static.

Two things have to change together. .experience is align-items:start, so .viewer shrink-wraps its content and a sticky television inside it would have almost no travel; .viewer needs align-self:stretch to give the sticky element the row's height to move through. And the television is 689px tall against a 620px viewport, so pinning it without a height cap would clip the bottom of the screen -- worse than the scrolling it fixes. The canvas keeps its 5:4 ratio by capping WIDTH from the available height rather than setting max-height, which would squash it: chrome measures 92px, so max-width is (100vh - 124px) * 1.25, which stops binding on tall viewports where the column width is the smaller limit. A sticky element also needs a z-index or the status panel that follows it in the DOM paints over it.

spec: plan/phase-5-browser-and-deploy.md
-> /go-engineer
[TC-5.14]
close_reason: The desktop viewer now pins the screen, its status line and the reset as one sticky stage, so scrolling to the lower handset keys no longer takes the picture off the top. Measured before: at 1280x620 scrolled to the end, the canvas was 56 percent visible. Three things were needed and two of them were only found by looking: .viewer needed align-self:stretch or the sticky element had no travel; the stage is capped from the viewport height, applied as a max-width so the 5:4 ratio holds and the bezel shrinks with the picture rather than pillarboxing it; and nothing may sit below a pinned stage, because the screen-help copy scrolled under it and overprinted the reset note -- that copy moved up into the intro, and is hidden entirely in short landscape where 320px of height has no room for standing explanation. The stage is display:contents below 760px so the television keeps sticking against the grid exactly as it did before. TC-5.14 in tests/e2e/handset.spec.ts covers 1280x620 and 1440x900 and asserts the canvas is PINNED at the sticky offset, not just still visible -- without that assertion the test passed with position:sticky removed, because the height cap alone shortens the page enough to fit. Light and dark inspected at both sizes; mobile re-verified at 390x780; 19/19 Playwright, CSS lint clean.

title: [TASK-5.11] Reset the box from the page
description:
Host-level control on the browser page that restores the state the process started from, so a viewer meeting a stuck or halted box recovers it without an operator restarting the container.

Approach: a new client-direction 'reset' message in schema/wire.json (generated both sides; npm run wire:check enforces it), queued on the Transport and drained by runMachine at the same safe point keys are drained -- Runtime's contract admits only its instruction-loop owner to call Step/Restore/Compose, so the socket goroutine must never touch the board. The loop re-restores cfg.SnapshotPath through the existing box.Restore + acquiredSnapshot verification from phase 4, or rebuilds via board.New from verified flash where no snapshot is configured, then republishes a full frame and a state message. haltMachine currently pushes state and RETURNS, ending the goroutine permanently; the reset path must make a halted box runnable again or the control is useless in the one case it exists for.

Placement and honesty: the control sits away from the handset. web/index.html already ships a Standby key (data-raw=0xCC) which is a REAL guest key -- docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md measures 98 widgets and 22 blits on CC -- and a host reset next to it would read as a second copy of it. The same record warns that 'power_control is a device name, not evidence of standby', so there is no modelled power line: this is a host intervention and is reported as one, per the project's declared-intervention convention.

Shared box: one Runtime serves every viewer (per-viewer accounts are a rejected decision), so a reset is announced to all connected pages through the existing state message. Public surface: unauthenticated, so a server-side minimum interval between resets, and the phase-5 security audit is re-run because it currently certifies a surface with no state-changing control on it.

Interactive surface: the state matrix ships with this task, not as polish -- pressed, disabled while disconnected, no double-submit, outcome announced, keyboard and touch operable.

spec: plan/phase-5-browser-and-deploy.md
research: docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md (CC standby is a real guest key; power_control is a name, not standby hardware); internal/board/runtime.go (only the loop owner may Restore)
-> /go-engineer
[TC-5.13]
close_reason: Reset control shipped. A 'reset' client message in schema/wire.json (generated both sides) is queued on the Transport and drained by the instruction loop at the same safe point as keys, so Runtime keeps its single owner. It is accepted in EVERY phase -- the halted box is the case it exists for, and the phase gate that refuses keys would have refused it exactly there -- with a 3 s server-side minimum between restores and a matching client cooldown so a held-down button costs one rebuild. runMachine now owns a succession of boards: startBox is shared by startup and reset, so both land in the same state by construction, and a halt waits for a reset instead of ending the goroutine, which is what made a halted box recoverable at all. Announced to every connected viewer with a reason naming the host intervention and saying whether it restored the snapshot or cold-started from flash. The control sits outside #handset with a description distinguishing it from the guest's 0xCC standby key. Proven by cmd/goretrotv/reset_test.go against real firmware (halt -> reset -> ready, falsified against the old halt-returns behaviour), internal/web/transport_test.go (phase exception and rate limit, both falsified against real mutations -- the rate-limit test passed without a rate limit until it was rewritten to drain between presses), and tests/e2e/reset.spec.ts (full state matrix, 6 cases). Light/dark/390px screenshots inspected; no horizontal overflow; 140x44 target. go test -race ./..., ctl.sh lint, wire:check, typecheck, CSS lint and 17/17 local Playwright all pass. TC-5.13.

title: Investigate intermittent live Sky-to-menu timeout
description: Local npm run test:e2e:live against the verified private post-acquisition snapshot intermittently reports Ready and acknowledges a Sky click, but the framebuffer remains one colour for the entire 45-second menu wait. Other runs reach the exact Box Office hash in about 4 seconds. Determine whether this is host instruction throughput, CSI key scheduling, or guest state; capture retired count and key delivery on a failing run, then fix the product or test timeout according to measured cause. Acceptance: repeated isolated real-firmware runs pass and a negative control still fails when Sky delivery is withheld.
notes:
2026-09-20 measurement from the LIVE public container (goretrotvdemosrvuk-goretrotv-1, up 3 days, build 53c7d94-dirty): the box is NOT halted and NOT wedged -- it is running the guest idle loop (PC oscillating in 0x800E1B5C..0x800E1B78) at retired=836.5e9. What is wrong is THROUGHPUT. The 'guest progress' debug line prints every 5,000,000 instructions and the lines are 1.0-2.5 s apart, i.e. ~2.5-3.3M instructions/s sustained; 836.5e9 over 3 days averages ~3.2M/s. Spike 001 measured a 44.2M/s floor for the interpreter, and NFR was set at 15M/s. So the deployed box is running roughly 14x slower than the measured floor and below its own NFR. It is not CPU starvation: docker stats shows the container taking 112% CPU (1.1 cores) while the 12-core host is at load 10. Cause NOT yet determined -- candidates not yet discriminated: per-500k-instruction full-frame Compose in publishFrame, DEBUG log level in production, the container's CPU share, or a real interpreter regression since the spike. This is the likeliest explanation of the intermittent 45 s Sky-to-menu timeout: at ~3M/s a menu that takes 4 s on a good run is near the timeout on a bad one, so the flake is a throughput distribution and not a key-delivery bug. Next step is to discriminate those candidates by measurement (bench the interpreter alone, then with publishFrame, then at INFO level) before changing anything. Do not raise the test timeout until the cause is known.
2026-09-20 CAUSE LOCALISED, and three of the four candidates in the previous note are ELIMINATED. Measured three ways on this host: (1) the deployed container ~3.2M instr/s; (2) the SAME binary run NATIVELY, no container, no Traefik, debug logging on: 3.9M instr/s; (3) a bare Go test loop calling box.Step() on the restored snapshot with no transport, no logging and no frame composition at all: 3.2M instr/s, and adding a full Compose() every 500,000 instructions changed it to 3.6M/s, i.e. not measurably. So it is NOT the container, NOT host CPU contention, NOT DEBUG log level, and NOT publishFrame. The cost is inside board.Step() itself. Against spike 001's measured 44.2M/s interpreter floor and the 15M/s NFR, the assembled board retires ~3.2M/s -- 14x under the floor and 5x under its own NFR. TWO READINGS REMAIN OPEN and they are not the same bug: either the spike measured a bare CPU interpreter without the bus and the device pumps, so the ASSEMBLED board was always this slow and the NFR was never actually met (a measurement scope error in the spike), or something in Step regressed since. Do not raise the live test timeout on either reading. Next measurement is a CPU profile of that bare loop -- StepWithHooks advances the icount clock scheduler once per instruction and checks DMA.Fault and I2C.Fault every instruction, which is where I would look first, but that is a HYPOTHESIS and the profile is what settles it. This is also the user-visible complaint: 'the screen still seems stuck, pressing sky does nothing' (2026-09-20). It is not stuck -- at 3.2M/s the menu that the live spec sees in ~4s on a good run simply takes long enough to read as dead.
2026-09-20 PROFILE. Bare restored-snapshot step loop benchmarks at 191.6 ns/instruction (5.2M/s). CPU profile of that loop:

  StepWithHooks                     10.78% flat, 72.35% cum
  cpu.StepWithInterruptBoundary      9.02% flat, 25.10% cum   <- the actual CPU work
  mallocgcSmallScanNoHeaderSC5       9.02% flat, 14.31% cum   <- called 100% from StepWithHooks
  clock.Advance                      2.55% flat,  9.22% cum
  defer machinery (nextDefer,
    popDefer, deferprocStack)        ~6.3% flat

VERIFIED CAUSE, not a hypothesis: board.StepWithHooks does r.hooks = &hooks, which makes the StepHooks parameter escape. 'go build -gcflags=-m' says plainly 'internal/board/runtime.go:192:33: moved to heap: hooks'. Step() calls StepWithHooks(StepHooks{}) once per instruction, so the emulator performs ONE HEAP ALLOCATION PER EMULATED INSTRUCTION, plus a deferred closure to clear the field. The profile's malloc node is reached only from StepWithHooks, which corroborates it.

A RED HERRING I nearly filed as a finding: the same profile shows crypto/sha256 and runtime.memmove high in the flat list. They are NOT in the instruction loop -- peeking their callers gives firmware.hashes, snapcodec Reader/Writer, memory.RAM.Restore and io.ReadAll, i.e. the benchmark's firmware load and snapshot restore. b.ResetTimer() does not reset the CPU profiler, so setup is inside the profile. Reading the flat list without the callers would have sent the next person optimising the hashing.

Correcting my own earlier note: I guessed DMA.Fault/I2C.Fault checks per instruction were the first place to look. They do not appear meaningfully in the profile. The allocation and the defer do.

SIZING, so nobody expects too much: the CPU core is only about a quarter of the loop, so removing ALL of the board wrapper's overhead lands somewhere near 20M instr/s, not 44M. That is over the 15M/s NFR but still well under spike 001's figure, which continues to suggest the spike measured a narrower thing than the assembled board. Do not close this by hitting 15M and declaring the spike met.
2026-09-20 CORRECTION TO MY OWN CONCLUSION, from the post-deploy check on the live host. I wrote earlier in this bead that the ~3.2M instr/s throughput was 'also the user-visible complaint' and that at that speed the menu 'takes long enough to read as dead'. THAT INFERENCE IS WRONG and the measurement that kills it is simple: on the freshly deployed public box, clicking sky produced the Box Office menu in 0.3 SECONDS, and a reset restored the startup screen in 0.8 s. The menu costs on the order of a million instructions, not tens of millions, so 3.2M/s is quick enough for it either way.

What remains TRUE and measured: the assembled board retires ~3.2M instr/s against a 15M/s NFR, caused by a per-instruction heap allocation in StepWithHooks (gort-4sx.27). That is a real defect. What is NOT established is that it causes either this bead's intermittent 45 s timeout or the 'pressing sky does nothing' report. I connected the two because they appeared in the same session, which is the same shape of error this project already has on record: the measurement was real and the sentence attached to it described something nobody had checked.

The likelier explanation for the user's report, still unproven: the public box is shared and long-lived -- it had been up three days -- so visitors leave the guest on whatever screen they reached, and sky pressed from some of those screens does nothing visible. There was no way back from that state before the reset control existed, which is why the control was the right thing to build regardless of the throughput.

For THIS bead the question is therefore still open, and narrower than it looked: what makes a FRESH box, restarted from the snapshot by test:e2e:public, occasionally take more than 45 s to do a thing that normally takes 0.3 s. That is a 150x outlier, not a gradual slowness, so a throughput fix will not close it. Next measurement should capture retired count and CSI delivery on a FAILING run specifically -- the instrumentation added to the debug path on 2026-09-17 is there for exactly this and has not yet caught a failure.
2026-09-20, after gort-4sx.27 shipped: this bead is deliberately NOT blocked on the throughput work, and a dependency to that effect was added and then removed. The allocation fix is real -- 3.2M to 6.90M instr/s end to end -- but the retraction earlier in these notes stands: a freshly deployed box reaches the Box Office menu 0.3 s after sky, so throughput was never a plausible explanation for a 45-second timeout, and making the box twice as fast does not close this. The open question is unchanged and still narrow: what makes a FRESH box, restarted from the snapshot by test:e2e:public, occasionally take more than 45 s to do a thing that normally takes well under a second. That is a 150x outlier, not slowness. The debug instrumentation added on 2026-09-17 (retired count, csi_pending, frame hash every 5M instructions) exists to catch it and has not yet caught a failing run.
2026-09-20, observed on the LIVE public box (build 3e750be, post-allocation-fix, ~8.75M instr/s): two identical sequences minutes apart, reset -> wait 4s -> press sky -> wait 6s. The FIRST reached the Box Office menu (aria-label read back the six rows). The SECOND left the canvas on the plain blue screen, unchanged, and a subsequent Right and Left changed nothing either -- the same frame hash fc76f885 across all three waits. So it is reproducible in the wild on a fast box, which kills the last of the throughput explanation: at 8.75M instr/s the menu that normally appears in 0.3 s had 6 s and did not come. The distinguishing variable in both runs was a RESET immediately before, which is new since 2026-09-20 and was not present when this bead was filed -- worth checking whether a rebuilt board drops the first key, e.g. a key queued while the loop is between boards, or CSI state that the restore does not re-arm. That is a hypothesis; the next step is still to capture retired count and csi_pending on a failing run rather than to reason about it.

title: Research guest text and selected widget state for accessible screen descriptions

title: GATE: Go toolchain upgraded before goretrotv.demosrv.uk is published
description:
A PRECONDITION OF PUBLICATION, not a nice-to-have. Carried from the phase 1 security audit (plan/security-audit-phase-1.md, section 3), whose reachability triage changed what the numbers mean.

THE FACT THAT CHANGES THE DECISION. govulncheck reports 29 standard-library vulnerabilities this tree CALLS. Four of them are fixable within the Go 1.22 line. The auditor triaged all 29 by REACHABILITY FROM ATTACKER-CONTROLLED BYTES rather than by static call-graph 'called', and the result inverts the obvious reading:

- 6 IDs execute on attacker bytes AT THE LISTENER -- GO-2026-3563 (chunked request smuggling), 6089 (h2c preface timeout), 5039, 4601/4010 -- plus 1 more reachable only with pprof enabled (4341, via pprof.Profile -> FormValue).
- The other 22 are TLS/x509/DNS/OS machinery this program never enters.
- **ALL FOUR of the 1.22-fixable IDs fall in the UNREACHABLE buckets. Every single wire-path ID needs Go >= 1.23.8.**

So the patch bump from 1.22.2 to 1.22.12 that looked like the actionable mitigation buys NOTHING on any path an attacker can reach. It is worth doing for hygiene; it is not a security answer. The only real answer is a newer toolchain.

WHY THIS BELONGS TO PHASE 5 SPECIFICALLY. Today nothing is published: the listener binds loopback, the stack is not running, and those 6 wire-path IDs have no wire. Phase 5 is the phase that puts an HTTP surface on a public host at goretrotv.demosrv.uk behind Traefik. THAT is the moment the reachable six stop being theoretical. Publishing on Go 1.22 means publishing with six known, called, attacker-reachable standard-library vulnerabilities and no patch available in the line.

WHAT TO DO: upgrade the host and CI to a Go the wire-path IDs are fixed in (>= 1.23.8; prefer current stable), rebuild the baseline from the OLDEST toolchain then in use so it stays a superset, and confirm the reachable six leave the called set. NOTE the host constraint recorded in docs/decisions/0001-scaffold.md: this machine cannot fetch a toolchain (dl.google.com unreachable) and its Go comes from the distro, so this needs action outside the sandbox -- which is exactly why it is a gate rather than a task someone can quietly skip.

ALSO RECOMMENDED by the auditor, cheap and separate: move the reachability triage table INTO tools/govulncheck-baseline.txt. Today --write-baseline rewrites the ID list wholesale with no per-entry reason, so the file cannot say WHY each entry is accepted -- and an accepted-vulnerability list that does not record its reasoning is one nobody can re-audit.

Blocks gort-4sx.5 (production Dockerfile/Traefik/TLS) and gort-4sx.6 (developer surfaces must not be published).
source: plan/security-audit-phase-1.md; gort-6ar.13; gort-6ar.21
notes:
CORRECTED AND MEASURED 2026-09-16: THE GO TOOLCHAIN CEILING WAS NEVER REAL, AND THIS ISSUE IS MUCH SMALLER THAN FILED.

WHAT WAS WRONG. The scaffold recorded that this host cannot fetch a newer Go, on the evidence of one failed command: a build against a 'go 1.25' directive returning 'download go1.25 for linux/amd64: toolchain not available'. That was the TEST's fault. 'go1.25' is not a release -- toolchain names carry a patch component. Since Go 1.21 toolchains are ordinary MODULES served by proxy.golang.org, which this machine reaches; dl.google.com is not involved.

MEASURED, not reasoned:
- GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.24.12 go version -> downloads and runs.
- Newest fetchable: go1.27.1.
- Under GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.1, with go.mod UNTOUCHED: go build 0, go vet 0, go test -race 0 across 14 packages.
- govulncheck under go1.27.1: 'No vulnerabilities found' -- 0 called, down from 29, including all six that execute on attacker-controlled bytes at the listener.

SO THE WORK IS SMALL AND NEEDS NO ADMIN RIGHTS -- no sudo, no apt, no host change:
1. go.mod: raise the 'go' directive from 1.22 to the chosen version.
2. Remove 'export GOTOOLCHAIN := local' from the Makefile and GOTOOLCHAIN=local from the Dockerfile -- those are what pin it. They were added deliberately to make an accidental higher directive fail loudly rather than hang; that rationale dies with the ceiling.
3. Dockerfile builder: golang:1.22 -> the chosen version.
4. CI: raise setup-go's version to match, and keep CI and the host on the SAME version so the baseline stays a superset.
5. Rebuild tools/govulncheck-baseline.txt -- it should become empty. Keep tools/vulncheck.sh: it still answers 'anything new?' and its json-exit-0 guard is still correct.
6. Un-pin govulncheck from v1.1.4 (that pin existed only to build under 1.22).
7. CLAUDE.md says 'Go 1.22+' -- raise it, or it will be read as a ceiling by the next agent exactly as it was by this one.

CHOOSING THE VERSION: apt also offers golang-1.23 (1.23.1) and golang-1.24 (1.24.4), but the module-proxy route is better -- no root, and the version is pinned in go.mod where it is reviewable and reproducible for every agent and for CI. Prefer current stable.

STILL A PUBLICATION PRECONDITION, for the reason originally filed: today the six wire-path vulnerabilities have no wire, and phase 5 gives them one. The upgrade is now cheap enough to do much earlier -- ideally before phase 2 starts, so the CPU core is written and measured on the toolchain it will ship on.
close_reason: Go 1.27.1 pinned in module, CI and Docker; build, image, race tests, lint, 7 conformance rules/21 probes, and govulncheck zero called findings passed. Commit 1ee1120.

title: The Go emitter must never sample between a branch and its delay slot (carried from phase 1)
description:
CARRIED FROM PHASE 1 as a design constraint with NO COMMITTED ENFORCEMENT. Surfaced by p1-qa auditing TC-1.6, settled by p1-core in commit 5c02f82 ('The straddle becomes a POSITIVE test, and the port is the side that conforms'), and recorded here because phase 1 had no CPU to enforce it against.

THE CONSTRAINT. The oracle retires a branch AND its delay slot in one loop iteration, so it steps over the checkpoint boundary: 477 of 4,629 checkpoints on the recorded cold boot land off-boundary (about one in ten), the first at its FOURTH checkpoint. THE PORT IS THE SIDE THAT CONFORMS -- the oracle is the reference and editing it to agree with the port is the move that destroys its value. So the Go emitter must observe at the same instants the oracle does, and must NEVER sample mid-pair.

WHY MID-PAIR IS NOT MERELY DIFFERENT BUT WRONG: between a branch and its delay slot the machine state is incomplete -- the pending branch target and the MIPS16 delay flag are not folded into the hash. A hash taken there does not describe a state either implementation can be at. This is the same rule the interrupt path already follows.

WHAT HAPPENS IF THIS IS GOT WRONG: oraclecmp no longer STOPS on such a window (that was gort-6ar.26, fixed), but it still cannot compare it -- it counts it, names it and carries on. So a port that samples mid-pair does not fail loudly; it quietly makes a growing fraction of the boot incomparable, and FR-6's coverage erodes without any gate going red. On the recorded boot that would be one window in ten, invisible.

WHERE IT BITES: TASK-2.2 (the instruction loop) and TASK-2.9 (drive the first divergence to zero). TASK-2.9 in particular cannot mean anything if the two sides sample differently -- its whole premise is that a remaining divergence is a CPU defect rather than a sampling artefact.

WHAT TO BUILD: a committed check that the Go emitter's checkpoint icounts are reachable sampling points, not mid-pair. The cheapest form is asserting that no checkpoint is emitted while a branch is pending. WATCH IT FAIL: sample deliberately mid-pair and confirm the check goes red, then restore -- and per the phase's own hard-won rule, the control must fire on an input the real loop can produce and against a value the test environment does not supply for free.

source: plan/test-plan-phase-1.md TC-1.6; gort-6ar.26; commit 5c02f82
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason: Core.ObserveCheckpoint skips pending branch slots; committed test drives an actual branch/slot loop and confirms a deliberately raw mid-pair sample is detectable. Race suite and lint pass.

title: The two emitters sample at different instants, so a live oracle-vs-Go comparison dies at checkpoint 4
description:
FOUND BY p1-qa, CONFIRMED BY THE LEAD IN THE CODE. This is the one that stops FR-6 doing its job, and it is upstream of oraclecmp rather than in it.

THE FACT. The real oracle stream has 478 of 4,934 checkpoints landing OFF-BOUNDARY (300001, 1000001, 1500001, ...) -- about 10%, and the FIRST is at the 4th checkpoint. The MIPS32 path retires a branch and its delay slot in one loop iteration and steps over the interval boundary.

THE BEHAVIOUR. compare.go pairs by WINDOW correctly (no WindowMissing). But having paired, compare.go:191 does 'if ca.ICount != cb.ICount -> CadenceDiverged' and RETURNS BEFORE COMPARING HASHES. Verified with a synthetic straddle carrying IDENTICAL hashes (300000 vs 300001): exit 1, 'cadence diverged at window 3 ... go reached instruction 300000, oracle reached 300001'.

THE CONTRADICTION. compare.go:114's own doc comment says demanding equal instruction counts 'would report a divergence at the first straddling branch between two machines that agree perfectly'. The code does exactly that, one scope inward. TestADifferentInstructionCountInTheSameWindowIsItsOwnKindOfDivergence pins the behaviour, so the test enshrines it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND PHASE 1. On a live oracle-vs-Go run, oraclecmp exits 1 at checkpoint 4 and NEVER REACHES a state comparison. So gort-6ar.25's committed live comparison cannot mean anything, and phase 2's 'drive the first divergence to zero' has no instrument to drive. FR-6 is the project's only independent correctness check and it is currently unable to compare the two machines at all.

THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE VALUABLE PART, and it is p1-qa's: THE COMPARATOR IS HONEST. A hash taken after 300,001 instructions is not comparable to one taken after 300,000, so 'cadence diverged' is the truthful answer GIVEN THOSE INPUTS. No comparator can rescue it. The defect is that the two emitters SAMPLE AT DIFFERENT INSTANTS.

REJECTED FIX: making oraclecmp tolerate a +1 skew. That compares different instants and calls it agreement -- it would turn the project's only independent check into one that cannot see a real one-instruction divergence. p1-qa refused to tick it on that basis and is right.

THE TWO REAL OPTIONS, for p1-core to choose and justify:
(a) The ORACLE samples at the exact boundary -- hash before retiring the delay slot when the branch crosses it.
(b) The GO side adopts the oracle's retirement granularity, so both land on the same instants.

GOVERNING CONSTRAINT: the oracle is the REFERENCE and the port conforms to it (CLAUDE.md: editing the oracle to agree with the Go port is the one move that destroys its value). That points at (b). If (a) is nonetheless correct -- and it may be, since stopping between a branch and its delay slot is a legitimate architectural state with the BD bit set, so sampling there is defensible as making the instrument sample at a DEFINED point rather than as making it agree -- then it must be argued on that ground, and proved inert against existing probes exactly as TASK-1.9 was (before/after baseline, anchored on figures the record states independently).

Whichever is chosen, the fix must make the straddle case a POSITIVE test: two agreeing machines that straddle a boundary must compare EQUAL, not merely fail differently.

BLOCKS gort-6ar.25 (the committed live comparison) and should be resolved before phase 2 (gort-dji) starts its divergence work.

OWNERSHIP: p1-core -- internal/platform/statehash, cmd/oraclecmp, reference/digibox-boot.html.
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason: Fixed (commit 0f2dc1f). The comparison no longer returns at the first window where the instruction counts differ: it counts such windows, notes them, and carries on, reporting BOTH the first disagreement of any kind AND the first window where both reached the same instruction count and their states differed. Hashes are still NOT compared across different instants - that would manufacture a false finding - but that no longer stops the instrument. oraclecmp prints both, says how many windows were incomparable and why, and points tier 2 at the STATE divergence rather than at the straddle. Proved on the real recorded boot: a simulated port stream with all 477 off-boundary checkpoints moved onto their boundaries plus one genuine state difference at instruction 200,000,000 now reports the straddle at window 3 AND finds the state divergence at window 2000, 4,151 windows agreed, 477 named incomparable; before it stopped at window 3. Four mutations each watched, including returning at the first straddle (the shipped bug itself) - note one mutation attempt was a no-op because 'break' inside a 'switch' breaks the switch, and it SURVIVED until the mutation was fixed. Compared now counts the whole shared range rather than the prefix, because stopping early made that number mean 'agreed before I stopped looking'. The emitter gains the upstream contract as documentation: both sides must sample at the same instant, never between a branch and its delay slot - the same rule the interrupt path follows, and the state mid-pair is not well defined since the pending branch target is not in the hash. Also fixed two tests that were passing on luck: TC-1.6's injected corruption was an XOR applied every instruction (toggling back and forth) and then an OR that was a no-op; it now writes COP0 12, which the toy program never touches.

title: Phase 1: Foundation: scaffold, CI, bus/device, and the ORACLE checkpoint machinery
description: Plan: plan/phase-1-foundation.md. Test plan: plan/test-plan-phase-1.md
close_reason:
PHASE 1 COMPLETE. All 15 planned tasks, plus 13 follow-up issues the build itself surfaced, plus five gates. Every child closed -- bd's refusal to close an epic over an open child was never overridden and nothing was detached or forced.

THE PHASE DELIVERED WHAT ITS OUTCOME ASKED: every later phase can build, test, deploy and observe, and CAN BE CHECKED AGAINST THE ORACLE FROM ITS FIRST INSTRUCTION. FR-6's instrument works -- verified by the lead against the real recorded boot, not by reading a report: 4,629 checkpoints agree with themselves (exit 0), a truncated stream is a HARNESS FAILURE and not agreement (exit 2, keyed off the END trailer's absence), and a planted divergence at instruction 200,000,000 is localised to window 2000 with tier 2 pointed at the state divergence rather than the sampling question.

MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the oracle is deterministic with respect to icount over a full cold boot with the broadcast silenced -- two boots agree over 4,613 checkpoints / 461M instructions, with 4,934 DISTINCT hashes so agreement is not the degenerate constant-hash case. That converts an architecture rationale (drive everything off icount) into a demonstrated property. Explicitly NOT established with the broadcast on.

THE DEFECT SHAPE THIS PHASE EXISTS TO HAVE LEARNED, found SEVEN times across three agents, three packages, a gate, a CI step, a git config and the lead's own verification script: A CHECK THAT CANNOT RUN LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE A CHECK THAT PASSED. Instances: a snapshot contract check passing a device that forgot a field (the mutator left it at its fresh value); a census reporting a confident zero over an empty population; ./ctl.sh lint reporting a pass while skipping twelve linters; git silently running NO hooks when core.hooksPath pointed nowhere; a boot-gate stage asserting non-emptiness against linker defaults that are never empty; a handler test with the same defect, whose FIRST repair was also satisfied by construction; and a layer-boundary check matching Go's own internal/cpu and reporting five false positives.

THE RULE, in the form it took three failed repairs to reach: A CONTROL MUST BE ABLE TO DISTINGUISH -- it must fire on an input the real system can produce, AND against a value the test environment does not already supply for free. You can watch something fail and still have watched the wrong thing.

WHAT MADE THE DIFFERENCE: every significant defect was caught by someone who did not build the thing. QA on a different model found the straddle that would have ended every live comparison at checkpoint four, and corrected a drift-guard claim that had already propagated two levels up. The security audit on a different model proved the loopback negative and found an unrecoverable OOM in a shared primitive. The lead found the decorative gate stage by driving the gate rather than reading its report. And this gate caught the auditor's own marker/report disagreement.
