description: External prerequisites. Assigned to the owner; everything edged here waits on them.

title: [TASK-7.14] Idling before a key press loses the key, and nobody knows why
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-23, and the numbers are not marginal.

TestWhatHoldsTheRowCountOnAListScreen ran eight million instructions of nothing between a settled screen and the next key press -- a hand-rolled way of letting the last screen finish, from before pressAndLetItFinish existed. With that idle in place, every LEFT from a settled box office menu was swallowed:

    box office (six entries)      A6A21DC5 -> FE8D1CCC   over 25707 addresses
    left to the tv guide menu     FE8D1CCC -> 00000000   over  6688 addresses
    left to the tv guide menu     FE8D1CCC -> 00000000   over  4736 addresses
    left to the tv guide menu     FE8D1CCC -> 00000000   over  4814 addresses

Delete the idle and the same press lands first time:

    left to the tv guide menu     FE8D1CCC -> 43779DC8   over 24957 addresses

The probe went from failing after 193 seconds to passing in 18.

THE 'FROM' HASH IS WHAT PROVES IT IS THE KEY AND NOT THE DETECTOR. The screen before the SECOND press was still FE8D1CCC, so the first press had not moved it either -- this is not a draw the settle detector missed, the box genuinely did not act. The address counts say the same thing from the other side: a press that lands touches ~25,000 distinct DRAM addresses, a swallowed one ~5,000, which is a box sitting still.

WHY IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and it matters which of these it is:

  - THE CSI MODEL. internal/device/csi holds a key code for the guest to read. If the model expects the guest to consume it within some window, or if the key's press-and-release is modelled with timing this port gets wrong, then idling past that window drops it -- and that would be OUR bug, in the one device that stands between a viewer and everything else.
  - THE FIRMWARE. A real Digibox may genuinely ignore a key when its menu task has gone quiescent, in which case this is correct behaviour and the lesson is only about how probes drive it.

Distinguishing them is one probe: watch the CSI registers and the guest's reads of them across an idle-then-press, and compare with press-immediately. If the guest never reads the key, the model dropped it; if it reads it and does nothing, the firmware did.

Until then every probe presses without idling, which is what the suite now does.

-> /go-engineer  [no-test: the acceptance IS a firmware probe naming which of the two it is]

title: [TASK-7.13] The 0xC1 extension sweep stopped discriminating once the 0xB2 shipped
description:
TestWhichPIDAndExtensionTheTableC1ConsumerWants passed at 7ed8ca2 and fails from 07981cc 'Broadcast the 0xB2 descriptor' onward, with byte-identical numbers across every run since:

    extension 0041 ->  639 exclusive PCs   (a LETTER: A)
    PID 0x52 ext 0x0100 -> 1362 exclusive PCs
    PID 0x11 ext 0x0100 ->  808 exclusive PCs   (wrong PID)
    PID 0x52 ext 0x0200 ->  826 exclusive PCs   (extension outside 0x0000/0x0100)

Its own guards fire: 'the wrong PID woke 808 against the target's 1362 -- too close to call the addressing established' and 'an extension outside 0x0000/0x0100 woke 826 against the target's 1362 -- the extension no longer discriminates'. TestTheIndexDispatchBoundariesAreWhereTheDecompilerSaysTheyAre fails the same way (0x01D0 woke 826 against 0x01CF's 1357).

THE PROBE IS BEHAVING CORRECTLY AND ITS MEASUREMENT IS NO LONGER SOUND. The 0xB2 gave every menu more to paint, so the FLOOR of work a run does went up and the exclusive-PC margin between a section the box wants and one it does not has closed. That is a property of the instrument's method, not of the 0xC1 consumer -- nothing about the index changed.

WHAT TO DO IS A MEASUREMENT DECISION, not a threshold tweak. The eventinfo probe shows the method still works when the comparison is honest: TestWhatTheBoxDoesWithThePresentFollowingEIT runs the SAME schedule twice as a control and gets a noise floor of exactly ZERO, because this emulator is deterministic. These sweeps compare runs with DIFFERENT broadcasts and no control at all, so their floor is whatever the extra sections cost. Give them a same-schedule control run and measure the margin against that, the way eventinfo does.

Do NOT relax the guard to make the probe green: the guard is the only thing that noticed.

-> /go-engineer  [no-test: the acceptance is the probe passing with a control and reporting the same conclusion]
close_reason:
Fixed and verified 2026-09-23. The differential is now taken against a delivery the box REFUSES rather than against silence: signature = (accepted A n accepted B) \ (control u refused A u refused B), with a third refused extension -- which defined nothing -- reporting the floor. Two accepted extensions from different dispatcher arms (0x0000 and 'A') intersected leave what dispatching itself does; subtracting two refusals removes what arriving costs.

THE FLOOR IS ZERO and every verdict is a cliff: acceptance path 473 addresses, a refused delivery hits 0 of them. Letters 473/473; non-letters 0/473; 0x00FF 467/473; 0x0100 and 0x01CF 444/473; 0x01D0 0/473; the same section on PID 0x11 0/473. Every earlier conclusion survives and is now unambiguous -- 0x01CF against 0x01D0 is 444 against 0 where the old method gave 1357 against 826.

Both probes pass, separately and in one process (they share the signature through a sync.Once, which is also what keeps the cost to six extra acquisitions rather than twelve). The subject assertion was deliberately moved OUTSIDE that Once: t.Fatal inside one calls runtime.Goexit and Do marks itself done anyway, so a half-built signature would have been handed silently to the next caller and every case would have read as refused.

A sub-finding logged rather than asserted: the letters reproduce the path whole and the genre arm reproduces all but ~29 addresses, so those belong to the alphabetical family -- the same family split the record argues for on other grounds.

Recorded in docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md as 'The 0xC1 differential, re-based on a delivery the box refuses', anchored and stamped. The stale claim that this transmitter had never sent a 0xC1 is corrected where it sat, in the record and in tablec1_firmware_test.go. The guard was NOT relaxed.

title: [TASK-7.12] Two route helpers now pin the same screens; keep one
description:
openAllChannels (route_test.go) and openAllChannelsFinished (azroute_test.go) are the same route since the press pins were re-measured on 2026-09-23: both start at box office 0xFE8D1CCC, take ONE left to the TV GUIDE menu 0x43779DC8 and one SELECT. azroute's version was written precisely BECAUSE route_test.go's pins were mid-paint hashes; that reason is gone, and two helpers with the same behaviour is the parallel implementation the conventions forbid.

Keep openAllChannels, because it is the one every probe already calls and it carries the wantChange contract. Migrate azroute's callers (azPressFunc users: tunepids, nativecensus_az, eventinfo, and whatever else greps up), delete openAllChannelsFinished and azTVGuideMenu/azHighlighted/azCategoryMenu where they duplicate the shared constants.

WATCH THE GRID FILL. openAllChannelsFinished returns the screen SELECT produced, which is now 0x144CF59D 'Searching for listings' -- the grid fills about sixty million instructions later. A probe that tunes or measures from the returned hash must let it fill first; eventinfo_firmware_test.go has the measured wait and the picture that proves why (a SELECT pressed at the searching screen is consumed by the fill and returns the filled grid, which reads exactly like a tune).

-> /go-engineer  [no-test: the acceptance is the existing suite passing unchanged]

title: [TASK-7.11] Broadcast the genre index so the TV GUIDE's eight category screens fill
description:
The A-Z index is shipped and ALL PROGRAMMES A-Z draws real programmes. The SAME table feeds
the guide's genre screens and they are still unfed.

WHAT IS ALREADY ESTABLISHED (see gort-qxl.3 and the digibox-emulation record):
  - table 0xC1 on PID 0x52, consumer 0x800C4C34, fully decompiled;
  - the dispatch's fourth arm is 0x0100..0x01CF, slot (ext & 0x0F) * 4 + ((ext & 0xC0) >> 6)
    -- SIXTEEN CATEGORIES BY FOUR SIX-HOUR BLOCKS, the same blocks a title table's low two
    bits select. Boundaries measured on the box: 0x01CF accepted, 0x01D0 rejected;
  - a record is rec[0..1] = listings id, rec[5..6] = event id;
  - one letter (or category) PER WAVE: a burst on one PID loses most of what it sends;
  - EVERY slot must exist, including empty ones -- the A-Z screen searched for ever with 19
    of 26 heads filled and 7 null. Expect the same for the 64 genre slots;
  - the guide's own string table names eight categories: MOVIES, SPORTS, ENTERTAINMENT,
    NEWS & DOCUMENTARIES, KIDS, MUSIC & RADIO, SPECIALIST, and ALL CHANNELS first.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and must be measured rather than assumed:
  WHICH NUMBER IS WHICH GENRE. The category is the extension's low nibble; nothing maps it
  to a name. Do NOT guess from the menu's order. The technique that solved A-Z answers it
  directly and cheaply: open a genre screen and watch WHICH SLOT IT READS -- the slot index
  IS the extension. internal/multiplex/firmwaretests/tablec1_whichslot_firmware_test.go is
  the pattern; gridslot_firmware_test.go shows the two exclusions required (the parser at
  0x800C4C34 and the FREE routine at 0x800C4F94 both read the heads constantly while the
  carousel delivers, and without excluding both the instrument reports the screen reading
  everything).

  Also unknown: whether the title record's Genre byte relates to the category number at all.
  It is transmitted and has never been read back.

NOTE the ALL CHANNELS grid is NOT one of these screens: it reads no 0xC1 slot at all
(17.8M data reads, none touching a head). Do not fold the two together.

spec: plan/phase-7-unsolved-screens.md
[no-test: the acceptance IS a firmware probe + screenshot, written as part of the task]
-> /go-engineer

title: Stop running the real-firmware tests under the race detector, or make them cheap enough to keep
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-22. internal/multiplex/firmwaretests costs 237s plain with the tests it had before that date, about 320s with the wedge guard and the card-policy arms added. One representative firmware test timed both ways gives the detector's multiplier: 60s plain, 507s under -race = 8.5x. So the package was ALREADY over the thirty-minute cap at 237 x 8.5 = 2015s before anything was added to it. The cap has now been raised to sixty minutes, which is the third raise and buys time rather than fixing anything.

THE DETECTOR ADDS NOTHING HERE, which is the actual argument. These tests drive a deliberately single-threaded emulator -- CLAUDE.md's own architecture decision is 'no goroutine in the instruction loop', and concurrency lives at the edges. Eight and a half minutes of CPU per test is being spent looking for data races in a loop that architecturally cannot have one. The races worth finding are in internal/web and the transport, which are cheap to run under it.

OPTIONS, none of them decided:
- Run -race over everything EXCEPT this package, and this package plain. Cheapest and matches where races can actually be.
- A build tag or a testing.Short()-style gate so the firmware boxes skip under -race the way they already skip under -short.
- Leave it and keep raising the cap. This is the status quo and it has now happened three times.

THINGS ALREADY TRIED AND MEASURED, so they are not worth repeating:
- A SHARED ACQUISITION across the twelve tests that each acquire the same fixture on the same day. Saved only ~26s, because runUntil already early-exits as soon as the block registers rather than spending its 120M budget. It also BROKE the A-Z test: the snapshot restores the box but the transmitter is a fresh Go object, so the two are out of step and the box behaved differently. Reverted. Making it sound would mean snapshotting the transmitter too, which is a bigger job than 26s is worth.
- SAMPLING THE FRAMEBUFFER LESS OFTEN in the press loop (65536 -> 262144 instructions). Made it WORSE, 507s -> 593s: a coarser sample means a press takes longer to be seen as settled, so each one runs more guest instructions. The cost is instruction execution, not hashing. Reverted.

So the cost is raw guest instructions under the detector, and the only levers are fewer instructions or no detector.

title: The TV GUIDE menu will not move its highlight past entry 6
description:
The TV GUIDE tab lists ten entries: ALL CHANNELS, ENTERTAINMENT, MOVIES, SPORTS, NEWS & DOCUMENTARIES, KIDS, MUSIC & RADIO, SPECIALIST, A-Z LISTINGS, PERSONAL PLANNER.

MEASURED 2026-09-22: the highlight moves down to entry 6 (KIDS) and stops. FORTY down presses moved it FIVE times and then nothing -- the screen hash was identical across the last thirty-five. That is not the key-swallow behaviour of gort-slq: thirty-five consecutive presses do not all get absorbed. The menu is refusing to go further.

So entries 7 to 10 are unreachable. That includes A-Z LISTINGS at entry 9, which is the screen the 0xC1 table feeds -- so the table can be LINKED into the box's A-Z index (proved: head[0x80120E10] points at our header) but the screen that would display it cannot be opened.

Artefact: .artifacts/tablec1-az-nav-stuck.png shows the highlight on entry 5 after eight presses.

THE NUMBER KEYS DO NOT WORK HERE EITHER. Pressing 0x09 left the highlight on entry 1 and the screen on the menu. lessons.md records that only four handset codes were ever proved against a screen (0x7D, 0x7E, 0x80, 0xF5) and the digits are not among them, so '0x09 means 9' is an assumption this menu does not support. Worth its own measurement: sweep 0x00..0x0F against a menu and see which codes move a highlight, the same way the four were established.

SAME FAMILY AS THE EMPTY GRID (gort-qxl.1): the screen exists, the box declines to enter it. Both are most likely the box having no data it considers valid for those entries, which would make this a symptom of the broadcast rather than of the menu -- but that is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

FIRST STEP: find what gates the highlight. A read-watch during a DOWN press at entry 6 should show the guest consulting whatever it checks before moving, the same way the 0xB1 entry layout was read.
close_reason:
WITHDRAWN as a mis-reading, and superseded by gort-slq.

Filed as 'the TV GUIDE menu will not move its highlight past entry 6'. It does not move past entry 6, but the menu is not what stops it: measured the same day, UP stops working as well, and so does box office, which leaves the menu entirely. The stop point also VARIES between runs -- five moves, then three -- which a disabled entry would not do.

At the wall Nucleus's TCD_Execute_Task [0x801072B0] reads zero and every guest task is blocked, while the box goes on retiring instructions in the idle loop. The box is WEDGED, and the menu not moving is one symptom of that rather than a gate on entries 7 to 10.

So there is nothing here to fix that is not gort-slq, which is raised to P1 and now carries the RTOS evidence and the task census. The A-Z LISTINGS screen remains unopenable, but for that reason and not this one.

The reproduction lives in internal/multiplex/firmwaretests/menustop_firmware_test.go.

title: [epic] Ideas: directions logged before they have a shape
description:
Ideas the owner has raised that are NOT yet buildable: no decided outcome, no known cost, and often re-opening a recorded decision. They are deferred so they stay OUT of bd ready, are never claimed and never estimated -- the size is unknown until a spec exists, which is what makes them ideas.

An idea LEAVES through /architect (and /spike where an assumption is load-bearing), then comes back through /feature-intake promote, which writes the phase file, the test plan and the tasks. The idea then closes pointing at where it went.

An idea filed as a task is the failure this epic exists to stop: it lands in the ready queue at the same priority as real bugs, looks startable, and gets built off a fag packet.

title: A halted box still answers /health ok, so the boot gate and every monitor miss it
description:
/health CANNOT DISTINGUISH A RUNNING GUEST FROM A HALTED ONE, so a halted box passes every automated check the project has. Found while driving the gort-sgc halt end to end on 2026-09-21.

MEASURED. A box was halted by a live schedule edit at 16:35:05.379 ("guest halted"). Twenty-two seconds later, at 16:35:27, /health answered:
  {"status":"ok","version":"dev","commit":"unknown","timestamp":"2026-09-21T16:35:27Z"}

CAUSE: internal/httpx/handlers/health.go:24-31 is a static handler. It writes status "ok" plus version, commit and a timestamp, and holds no reference to machine state at all. Nothing in the process narrows it after haltMachine runs.

WHAT THIS DEFEATS:
- ./ctl.sh health and ./ctl.sh health-public report a healthy box that is stopped.
- The BOOT GATE's liveness stage is this endpoint: tools/boot-gate.sh:162-205 asserts "health answers ok" (status == ok) and "health names this build" (commit matches HEAD). Both pass on a halted guest. The gate's own header at line 15 describes stage 4 as "/health answers, and NAMES THIS BUILD" -- an identity claim, which it does prove. It is not a liveness claim, and it is the only thing standing in that position.
- Any external uptime monitor pointed at the public URL.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DEFEAT: viewers DO see the halt -- haltMachine (cmd/goretrotv/main.go:465-470) pushes phase "halted" with the reason over the WebSocket, so a browser shows it immediately. The blindness is confined to the HTTP health surface, which is what automation watches.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND gort-sgc: this is not specific to schedule faults. ANY stopHalt -- a bad guest instruction, a snapshot restore failure, a rebuild failure -- leaves a process that serves a cheerful /health. CLAUDE.md's own rule is that a hardware model "fails by running for ever doing something plausible", and this is the monitoring equivalent: a green check over a stopped machine.

FIX DIRECTION (decide, do not assume): either have /health report the machine phase and answer non-200 when halted, or add a separate liveness assertion to the boot gate that proves the guest is retiring instructions -- e.g. the instruction count moving between two reads. Prefer the second if /health's build-identity contract is considered load-bearing for the deploy gate (phase 5's audit records that contract deliberately). Do NOT silently change /health's shape without checking tools/boot-gate.sh and the public Playwright checks that parse it.

title: The services key disconnects the viewer: 0x7E is on the page but not in handsetRaw
description:
The handset shows a `services` key the server refuses, and pressing it disconnects the viewer.

CONFIRMED ON THE LIVE PUBLIC DEMO 2026-09-21 (https://goretrotv.demosrv.uk, serving 47e1f01), by pressing the real button in a real browser and sampling #key-feedback every 200ms:
  t+200ms  "The handset is unavailable while disconnected."
  t+600ms  "The handset is ready."
The socket is closed by the server and the client reconnects about 400ms later.

MECHANISM:
- web/index.html:60 offers <button data-raw="0x7E">services</button>. Every handset button ships `disabled` and web/app.ts:46 ENABLES them all once the box is ready, so this is a live, clickable control for every visitor -- not a permanently disabled one.
- web/app.ts:238 sends Number("0x7E") = 126.
- internal/web/transport.go:341 decodeKey rejects it because handsetRaw (transport.go:360-369) allows 0x3c, 0x58-0x5c, 0x7d, 0x80, 0xcc, 0xf5, 0..9 and 0x6d-0x70 -- and NOT 0x7e.
- transport.go:257-258 closes the connection with StatusPolicyViolation "invalid key".

0x7E WAS NEVER IN THE ALLOWLIST: `git log -S"0x7e" -- internal/web/transport.go` is empty and the switch is unchanged since 1080fda. So the button and the allowlist have disagreed since the key was added to the page.

THIS CONTRADICTS THE PROJECT'S OWN RECORD, which states the handset answers exactly five codes INCLUDING 0x7E services (0x0C/0x80 tv guide, 0x7D box office, 0x7E services, 0xCC standby, 0xF5 interactive). Either the measurement is right and handsetRaw is missing a code, or the button should not be on the page. Do not guess -- measure which.

TRUST BOUNDARY: internet-reachable and unauthenticated, but FAIL-CLOSED and self-inflicted. The presser drops only their OWN connection; the box is NOT reset (resetState/runMachine at main.go:340-390 reset only on stopReset or a reset request) and other viewers are unaffected. Verified rather than assumed -- the shared-box concern was checked and does not hold.

Impact is therefore a user-facing defect on the public demo rather than a security breach: a visible control that disconnects you.

FIX (decide by measurement, do not guess): either add 0x7e to handsetRaw WITH a firmware test proving the box answers it -- the same standard every other key in that list was held to -- or take the button off the page. A third option, leaving it disabled, is not available: app.ts:46 enables the whole set.
notes:
RESOLVED WHICH SIDE IS WRONG -- no new measurement needed. lessons.md already records it, measured 2026-09-20 from the post-acquisition snapshot: raw 0x7E opens the Sky menu on the SERVICES tab, frame hash 64AF0A8D. (The same table corrects the old mis-attribution of 0x7E as 'the Box Office menu again', which happened because the original walk pressed it while the box was already showing Box Office.)

So the box DOES answer 0x7E and handsetRaw is simply missing it. The fix is to add 0x7e to the switch at internal/web/transport.go:360-369, with a firmware test asserting the 64AF0A8D frame -- the same standard the other four measured codes were held to. Do NOT remove the button.

Note while in there: lessons.md also records that the real Sky Rev 9 remote has 'sky' and 'box office' as SEPARATE buttons, so a distinct sky code exists and has not been found. That is a separate question and not part of this fix.
NOW ON THE CRITICAL PATH, not just a UI defect. 2026-09-21.

TestWhatReadsTheAssembledTableC1Array shows the box parses a 0xC1 section, allocates and assembles its array -- and then NOTHING reads it, across idle, tv guide, box office and interactive, 28 million instructions, with the bus observer proved (38,234 data reads seen over 200,000 instructions) and every copy in DRAM watched rather than the first.

The one screen that could not be tried is SERVICES, and lessons.md records raw 0x7E as exactly that -- the Sky menu's Services tab, measured against frame 64AF0A8D. It is unreachable because handsetRaw has never contained 0x7E. Pushing the key straight at box.CSI.Key would bypass the product path and prove nothing about it, so the test declines to and says why.

So fixing this unblocks a reverse-engineering question, not only a viewer-facing annoyance: it is the most plausible consumer of the 0xC1 table and the only reachable screen left untested.
close_reason:
Fixed: 0x7e added to handsetRaw (internal/web/transport.go), so the services key the handset has always offered now reaches the box instead of closing the viewer's socket with 'invalid key'.

THE JUSTIFICATION ALREADY EXISTED. handset_firmware_test.go has pressed 0x7E against the real firmware for as long as it has existed and asserts it draws its own distinct screen -- so 'the box answers 0x7E' was already proven, and the bead's request for a firmware test was asking for something the suite already had. What was missing was the connection: that test calls box.CSI.Key directly and never touches handsetRaw, so the page and the server could disagree indefinitely with both suites green. Which is precisely what happened, from the day the key was added.

SO THE GUARD CLOSES THE CLASS, NOT THE INSTANCE. internal/web/handsetpage_test.go reads web/index.html -- the page the product actually serves, not a list copied from it, because a copied list drifts exactly as this did -- extracts every data-raw code and asserts handsetRaw accepts it. Proved in both directions: with transport.go stashed it FAILS naming 0x7E and quoting the consequence; with the fix it passes. It also refuses to run silently if the regex stops matching (fewer than ten codes found is a harness failure).

Unit test updated too: decodeKey's documented-raws table now includes 0x7e.

WHAT IT UNBLOCKED, which is why this stopped being a UI defect: the Services screen was the likeliest consumer of the 0xC1 table and the only reachable screen left untested. It reads nothing -- so all five screens are now negative and the consumer is not a top-level screen at all. Recorded in docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md and on gort-qxl.3.

NOT DEPLOYED. The live demo at 47e1f01 still refuses 0x7E; this needs a release to reach viewers.

title: Validation is narrower than the builders, so a valid schedule can halt the box
description:
The reload validator is NARROWER THAN THE BUILDERS. A schedule that LoadListings accepts can be refused later by a section builder, and that refusal halts the guest. This defeats two claims the code makes in prose: listings.go:176 ("A MALFORMED EDIT KEEPS THE LAST GOOD SCHEDULE") and main.go:82 ("validated BEFORE the listener opens"). Both are true only to validate() depth.

MEASURED -- each of these is ACCEPTED by LoadListings and then REFUSED by a builder:
  channel 5000            -> BAT: channel 5000 exceeds twelve bits
  non-ASCII service name  -> SDT: non-ASCII printable byte at 3
  non-ASCII bouquet       -> NIT/BAT: non-ASCII
  300-byte service name   -> SDT: descriptor too long
  300-byte bouquet        -> NIT: network name too long
  86 services             -> NIT: service list descriptor too long | SDT: section length 1637 exceeds 1021
  all-unencodable channel -> records(): not even one programme fits in a title section
  250-char title          -> titles.go:112, does not fit one descriptor (100 chars fits)
And the bad edit is swapped in live: "Reload after channel=5000 edit: changed=true err=<nil>; live channel now 5000".

PROPAGATION (corrected -- an earlier note in this bead cited internal/board/runtime.go:221-224, which is the board's own AfterPump hook for Timer/CSI/modem/card, NOT this path):
  multiplex.go:259/263/267/366 -> carousel.go:177/191 -> multiplex.go:203
  -> cmd/goretrotv/main.go:428-429 return stopHalt, err
  -> haltMachine (main.go:352-357) pushes phase "halted" to every browser
On reset, transmitterFor (main.go:345) rebuilds over the SAME swapped guide, so it halts again at the next wave. It does not self-recover until the file is fixed.

ONE OVER-LONG TITLE DOES NOT HALT -- it is dropped silently at multiplex.go:449-451 (`continue`, no log). Measured: "one unencodable + one fine: err=<nil>, records kept=1 (of 2)". A viewer sees a gap in the guide and nothing says why. That is the second defect and it is separate from the halt.

TRUST BOUNDARY: operator-supplied file, mounted read-only in production (./listings:/listings:ro). NOT internet-reachable. Availability only, no data at risk.

FIX, both halves:
(a) Validate by construction. In LoadListings/multiplex.New, build NIT/SDT/BAT with a placeholder subscription and TitleSection per quarter, so reload keeps the last good schedule for everything the builders can refuse, and a bad file at startup fails by name.
(b) At main.go:428-429, log "transmitter off air" and set transmitter=nil instead of stopHalt -- the choice transmitterFor already makes at main.go:298-306. A schedule fault is a HOST fault; reporting it as a guest halt misattributes it to the firmware, which this project is careful about everywhere else.
Also log the dropped programme in (a) rather than dropping it silently.

Add regression cases to plan/test-plan-phase-6.md for: a builder-refused schedule keeping the last good one, and a dropped programme being named in the log.
notes:
HALT CONFIRMED END TO END ON REAL FIRMWARE, 2026-09-21. The chain is no longer read from code -- it was driven, with a control.

Method: the real binary on the real firmware, restored from snapshots/post-acquisition.snapshot, on 127.0.0.1:8100. Control and poison are BYTE-IDENTICAL schedules except for the titles of one existing channel -- same six channels, same ids, same times -- so the only variable is the thing under test.

CONTROL (listings/default.json unmodified), 45s:
  programmes on air | clock_waves:1 lineup_waves:1 title_waves:1 | no halt

POISON (Sky One's 18 titles replaced with 4000 chars each), 45s:
  16:33:38.599  broadcast loaded   channels:6 programmes:67   <- ACCEPTED at load, same counts as the control
  16:33:41.380  guest halted       broadcast: carousel title wave at 1112001536:
                                   multiplex: "Sky One": not even one programme fits in a title section

LIVE RELOAD -- the claim that actually matters, proved separately. Box started on the GOOD schedule, ran healthily, then the file was edited underneath it:
  16:34:44.752  programmes on air    (healthy, title_waves:1)
  16:35:04.855  schedule reloaded    (the edit was ACCEPTED and swapped in)
  16:35:05.379  guest halted         (same error)
524 MILLISECONDS from the reload accepting the edit to the box stopping. No restart involved.

TWO THINGS THE RUN ADDED THAT THE CODE READ DID NOT SHOW:
1. The log says "guest halted". The guest did nothing. A host-side schedule fault is reported as a firmware halt, which is exactly the misattribution this project avoids everywhere else -- and it is what someone debugging would chase first. This strengthens fix (b): go off air, do not stopHalt.
2. /health STILL ANSWERED ok 22 seconds after the halt. Filed separately as gort-f9w -- it is not specific to this bug and it means nothing automated notices any halt.

title: The broadcast carries today only, so the guide's next-block subscription goes unanswered after 18:00
description:
The guide registers TWO notification slots: the block its clock is in, and the one after it. Measured 2026-09-20 at 19:00 the second slot reads day+1 with tableIdLow 0 -- tomorrow's 00:00-06:00 block, because the block after 18:00-24:00 belongs to the next day.

The transmitter broadcasts the day the in-world clock is in and nothing else, so that second subscription is never answered. What a viewer would see: nothing at all before about 23:00 (NEXT is in the same block), then an empty NEXT late in the evening, and an empty guide for anyone who leaves the demo running across midnight until the clock's day rolls over and the line-up is re-sent.

The pieces are already there and measured: the box ARMS tomorrow's listings PID in the evening (multiplex.TitlePID of the next day -- 0x37 and 0x30 both armed on MJD mod 8 == 7), its own match unit asks for tomorrow as often as today after 18:00, and the guide directory already holds one schedule per date with default.json behind it. So this is 'send the next day's four blocks on the next day's PID when the clock is in the last block', not new measurement.

MEASURE BEFORE BUILDING: press tv guide at 23:00 and read what NEXT says. If the box fills it from its own store some other way, this is not worth building.

-> /go-engineer

title: [TASK-6.14] Huffman-encoded titles lose their spaces and gain a trailing character
description:
Every title on the guide renders without spaces and with an extra character: 'Dream Team' draws as DreamTeams, 'Walker Texas Ranger' as WalkerTexasRangers, 'A Live Edit While Running' as ALiveEditWhileRunnings. Readable but wrong, and it has been present since the first title section went on air -- it was invisible because every title tested happened to still be legible.

Both halves point at the same place. The space is almost certainly not being emitted by the encoder (internal/broadcast/huffman.go Encode/packHuffman), and the trailing character suggests the final partial byte is being padded with bits the decoder reads as one more symbol rather than as end-of-string.

The encoder already has a round-trip test against its own Decode, which is exactly why this survived: an encoder and a decoder that share a mistake agree. Cross-check against the reference decoder instead (that is TASK-6.9's cross-check), or read the drawn text off the framebuffer.

-> /go-engineer
[TC-6.14]
spec: plan/phase-6-broadcast.md
close_reason:
TASK-6.14 fixed: titles draw with their spaces and without the trailing character. Verified on the box's screen -- the guide now draws 'Dream Team' and 'Walker Texas Ranger' where it drew 'DreamTeams' and 'WalkerTexasRangers'.

TWO DEFECTS, both in reading the dictionary. (1) A value has MANY codes and only the shortest is real: SPACE appears 65 times in skyuk.dict, once as 110 and 62 times as 27-bit leaves that are the flattened tree's padding. A plain map assignment keeps the LAST, so every space went out as a filler the box does not decode back to a space. (2) THE PADDING IS DECODED -- the box reads a record to its declared length, not to the terminator -- and s is coded 0000, so zero-filling the last byte appended an s to every title. Padding is now the terminator's own bits truncated: every proper prefix of a code is a non-leaf, so it emits nothing.

A third thing fell out: openTVtoXML parses a single character BEFORE a phrase, which is what reads '==<bits>' as the code for '='. Cutting at the first '=' dropped it. Entry count 446 -> 447, MANIFEST updated.

THE METHOD NOTE IS THE POINT. All three were invisible to the round-trip test, to the byte-for-byte reference vectors, and to a decoder transcribed from the reference -- every one of those shares the encoder's reading of the dictionary. The old vectors were taken from a Python codec 'validated by round-tripping through a transcription of the reference decoder', which is an encoder checked against a decoder; its own comment warned about self-consistent wrongness while relying on it. Vectors regenerated and the provenance comment rewritten to say the authority is the screen.

title: Close the remaining gap to the 15M instr/s NFR
description:
The per-instruction heap allocation is gone (gort-4sx.27): 206.0 -> 94.75 ns/instruction, 3.2M -> 6.90M instr/s end to end. The NFR is 15M/s and the bare loop is ~10.6M/s, so the gap is real and this issue exists so it is tracked rather than quietly forgotten behind a satisfying 2x.

Where the time goes now, from the post-fix CPU profile, with the benchmark's own setup discounted: the CPU core (StepWithInterruptBoundary plus execute32) is about 45 percent of the in-loop cost, the bus read path about 13, the icount clock's Advance and schedule about 13, and StepWithHooks' own bookkeeping about 9. There is no single defect left of the kind 4sx.27 was -- closing this is ordinary optimisation with correctness risk on a hardware model, which is why it is P2 and not urgent.

WARNING for whoever profiles next: the profile's memmove and sha256 samples are the benchmark's firmware load and snapshot restore, NOT the loop. b.ResetTimer does not reset the CPU profiler. Peek the callers before optimising anything that looks hot; reading the flat list alone sends you to optimise the hashing.

Also unresolved and NOT the same thing: spike 001 measured 44.2M/s, which no amount of wrapper removal approaches. Either that spike measured a bare interpreter without the bus and the device pumps -- a measurement-scope error worth writing down -- or something else differs. Settling that is part of this issue, because the NFR was set from that spike.

Acceptance is a measurement against internal/board/step_bench_test.go's recorded 94.75 ns baseline, with the boot gate and the oracle gate still passing.
-> /go-engineer
[no-test: BenchmarkStep plus the existing boot and oracle gates are the check]
notes:
INVESTIGATED 2026-09-21. Three of this issue's own premises turned out to be wrong, one open
question is settled, and the obvious fix is blocked on a decision only the owner can make. Nothing
was committed to the loop: the attempt was reverted and the tree is green.

1. THE SPIKE-001 QUESTION IS SETTLED, AND IT WAS NOT A MEASUREMENT-SCOPE ERROR.
This issue asked whether the 44.2M/s figure meant the spike "measured a bare interpreter without
the bus and the device pumps". .research/001-go-interpreter-throughput/FINDINGS.md says so itself,
in bold, at the time: "It is an UPPER BOUND. No MIPS16 decode, no COP0 bookkeeping, no
per-instruction interrupt check, no peripheral dispatch on loads. A real core does all four, so
expect meaningfully less." The 15M/s NFR was then set DELIBERATELY below that ceiling with 40M as a
stretch. So the NFR is sound and the spike was labelled honestly; the question was answerable by
re-reading the spike. Close this sub-question.

2. THE 94.75 ns BASELINE IS NOT REPRODUCIBLE, WHICH BREAKS THIS ISSUE'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERION.
Nine runs today: 114.4, 117.2, 119.3, 119.4, 124.0, 124.3, 132.1, 135.0, 154.2, 176.9 ns/op. The
recorded baseline is 94.75. Nothing had changed. The cause is the HOST: load average 9.63 on 12
cores (postgres, php and cadvisor from other stacks, plus the goretrotv demo container legitimately
spinning a full core). taskset pinning to four cores did not fix it because the competing work is
not pinned away.
THE RECORDED BASELINE CARRIES NO RECORD OF THE CONDITIONS IT WAS TAKEN UNDER, so "a measurement
against the recorded 94.75 ns baseline" cannot be evaluated. Min-of-N is a usable estimator here
(114-117 across two independent sets) where the mean is not. Whatever lands next should record load
average and competing workload beside the number, or the next person repeats this.

3. THE RECORDED PROFILE BREAKDOWN IS WRONG ABOUT THE CLOCK.
This issue says "the icount clock's Advance and schedule about 13 percent". Measured under
StepWithHooks (i.e. in-loop only, with the benchmark's setup discounted as the issue's own warning
instructs -- and that warning is correct, 85 percent of the memory profile is Restore):
    cpu.StepWithInterruptBoundary   50.4% of in-loop
    clock.Advance                   31.0% of in-loop      <- not 13
    StepWithHooks flat              ~17%
    dma.Fault                        1.8%
Within Advance: the pump handler's own device work 48.6%, clock.add 11.4%,
runtime.mapdelete_fast64 11.4%, heap.Pop 2.9%.

4. THERE IS STILL A PER-EVENT ALLOCATION IN THE LOOP, contradicting "no single defect left of the
kind 4sx.27 was". internal/board/runtime.go registers the board pump as a ONE-SHOT THAT
RE-REGISTERS ITSELF every sixteen instructions (loopClock.At(now+16, ...) at the end of its own
handler). Each tick therefore allocates a fresh event, inserts it into the live map and deletes the
previous one. That is the 3 B/op the benchmark reports (31.5MB per 10M instructions, confirmed by
pprof -peek: clock.schedule <- Clock.At <- board.New.func1) and it is why mapdelete_fast64 is 11.4%
of Advance. The clock ALREADY supports periodic events, which reuse one event and touch neither map.
The board pump is the ONLY event on this clock, so the usual determinism worry about registration
-order tie-breaking does not arise here.

5. THE FIX IS BLOCKED ON A SNAPSHOT-COMPATIBILITY DECISION -- OWNER'S CALL.
Implemented it (a clock.EveryFrom(due, period, ...) so the first tick stays at instruction 1 and the
cadence stays 16, then registering the pump with it) and it FAILED CORRECTLY:
    TestPrivatePostAcquisitionSnapshotRestoresAndRuns: run-on state hash 9E6450C4, want 24B1489D
Cause, verified rather than guessed: Clock.Restore takes period FROM THE BLOB
(internal/platform/clock/snapshot.go:82,106), and snapshots/post-acquisition.snapshot was written on
17 Sep when the pump was a one-shot. Restored, it comes back with period 0; with the handler no
longer re-registering itself the pump fires ONCE AND STOPS. Correct on a cold boot, silently dead on
every existing snapshot. Reverted; internal/board, internal/platform/clock and internal/machine all
green again.

THE THREE WAYS FORWARD:
(a) Make the cadence belong to the CODE and the phase to the SNAPSHOT: machine.New takes a handler
    plus its period, and Clock.Restore uses the registered period with the blob's due. Old snapshots
    then work unchanged and the restored pump is periodic. Principled, and it is a change to the
    restore contract of the most safety-critical primitive in the project.
(b) Regenerate the post-acquisition snapshot. Cheap in code, but it invalidates a load-bearing
    private artefact and any recorded replay traces taken against it.
(c) Leave it. Honest expectation of the fix is SINGLE-DIGIT PERCENT -- it removes an allocation and
    two map operations per sixteen instructions, not per instruction.

SCALE, SO THE DECISION IS MADE ON NUMBERS: the loop needs about +40 percent to reach 15M/s from the
benchmark's ~10.6M/s recorded figure. The pump fix does not get there and nothing in the current
profile does: the CPU core is half the in-loop cost and there is no defect in it, just work.
Spike 001 already names the real lever for a step change -- "threaded dispatch or a JIT -- a
substantially larger piece of work, and explicitly not v1". If 15M/s is genuinely required, that is
the conversation, not this one.

title: [TASK-3c.9] Implement declared firmware application handoff policy
description: Match the browser oracle’s explicit deterministic handoff: when bootloader scheduler ready>=0x100 and current=0 for 200,000 retired instructions, verify flash JB magic against the ROM literal, set RA=0 and PC to the flash entry stub once. The guest must then execute the decompressor to 0x800009F4 and enter the application. No host image copy. Record exact policy firing and checkpoint trace; distinguish the host emulation step from guest execution. [TC-3c.7]
notes:
2026-09-17 diagnostic: Go/oracle checkpoint streams agree through 3.4M then differ at 3.5M because browser oracle forces host-side application PC handoff when ready=0x100/current=0; Go does not. Before fix, bootloader BOOTMain and EVTTask both blocked on EVTTick semaphore 0x8000A820 and no device raised board IRQ 0x40. Added guest-driven board timer B000D000, status +D0, ACK +E0, icount period 20k matching measured oracle: guest now advances BOOTMain and creates five bootloader tasks by 10M, EVTTask wakes periodically. At 100M BOOTMain status=2/suspended, flash descriptor step at 0x800050BC remains zero, scanner PC BFC122B6 and app entry BFC2048C never reached, main image 0x800009F4 still zero. Continue tracing BOOTMain suspension and bootloader update decision; do not close TC3c.7 or claim guest handoff.
Further trace after timer model: BOOTMain runs again at 8.138M and 31.054M; at 8.145379M it enters Nucleus sleep with argument 100 and status=2, then the event loop continues. It is a repeated guest sleep/poll path, not a dead semaphore wait. At 100M no PC BFC2048C, no image decomposition, no B200A000 read. docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md corrected to retract the earlier unproved claim that flash geometry was the located blocker. Timer commits 13ce6d2, 6b1a169; evidence correction 5c8bca1. Race tests, lint, nine-anchor CPU gate, boot gate, conformance 7/7 and 21/21 pass.
CSI wire diagnostic c12c997: at 100M guest transmits six complete command frames 0x11, 0x41, 0x52, 0x51, 0x10, 0x12, then no new frame. A trace with additional 0x12 ACK (default 0x52/0x18 plus 0x12) transmits the same six commands and still does not reach application entry by 100M. Thus missing ACK 0x12 alone does not prove the handoff blocker. Timer-driven scanner stop-PC BFC122B6 also did not fire by 100M.
Instruction watch d435d9c: reset copy at guest PC BFC18E58 writes [800050D0] from zero to A0001FE0 at instructions 3,100,879..3,100,897. The value is present at BOOTMain BFC012C6 at instruction 3,771,843; its only ROM literal is BFC01348, and the copied A0001FE0 value appears in U202 reset data at offset 0x1C8C0. Ghidra disassembly: BFC012C6 beqz to BFC012E6; nonzero calls BFC05C6C then cycles BFC012D4→sleep 500 ticks→BFC012E4 unconditionally, without rereading gate. Therefore waiting longer or ACKing CSI 0x12 cannot leave that branch; the unresolved question is why reset chose nonzero and what valid guest/hardware event can choose the zero path before this branch.
Independent read-only Ghidra trace confirms BOOTMain entry BFC01290. At BFC012C6, zero [800050D0] takes guest scanner path BFC012E6→BFC12790→BFC124F8→BFC122DC→BFC12298→BFC122B6; nonzero copied A0001FE0 enters unconditional BFC012D4..E4 service/sleep-500 loop. BFC01354 setup and one retry precede branch; no earlier image validation in BOOTMain. Runtime watch saw only reset-copy writes to gate before branch. No real device input known to choose zero. Docs/test-plan updated in ecac136; TC3c.7 remains open.
CORRECTION to prior notes and ecac136: BFC012C6 tests [800081F8], not [800050D0]. Runtime watch shows guest PC BFC00500 writes 0→1 at instruction 3,262,648; BOOTMain sees 1 and enters service/sleep loop. Reset copy to [800050D0] is real but unrelated to this branch; zeroing that word does not change path. Temporary host zero of actual gate at 9FC012C2 selects alternate path, sets flash descriptor step [800050BC]=0x10000, then stalls at guest PC 9FC028FA polling unmapped modem UART status B2001050 bit 0x40. At 100M no scanner BFC122B6, no app PC, image 800009F4 zero. These diagnostic host mutations are not acceptance. docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md and TC3c.7 corrected; actual guest cause of the gate write and required modem response remain under investigation.
2026-09-17 ROM self-test found: [800081F8] is result of BFC0B444 bus+demux test; earlier fixed1 came from demux channel5 not moving ROM TS bytes. Added DMA channel5 ROM/DRAM source transfer into demux TS parser, packed match-word readback, indirect configuration, CRC filtering, and boot section RAM writes. Normal guest now sets gate0 without host mutation, flash step [800050BC]=0x10000, and enters zero branch. Modem UART B2001000 is modelled; normal 10M no longer has unmapped B2001050 reads. BOOTMain next waits on CSI SMTAck for command0x44. Diagnostic -ack-code 0x44 reaches guest scanner PC 9FC122B6 at 19,193,163, but at100M application DRAM still zero and no handoff. Oracle 0x44 all-buttons-released reply is synthetic/inferred, not measured physical behavior; do not call this acceptance. Race tests, lint, cpu gate, boot gate, conformance pass after hardware model. Continue scanner/CSI investigation; TC3c.7 remains open.
2026-09-17 follow-up: diagnostic -ack-code 0x44 reaches scanner PC 0x9FC122B6 at 19,193,163 instructions and the scanner reads the JB header successfully. By 100M and 100.5M the machine is at the browser oracle's declared handoff boundary (ready=0x100,current=0) in the bootloader idle loop, but stop-PC probes for guest flash entry 0x9FC2048C and loader 0x9FC20618 do not fire and [0x800009F4] remains zero. 2026-09-17 user delegated acceptance choice toward the real-firmware, viewable-URL goal. Chosen policy: explicit oracle-style host PC handoff after guest-run validation and idle threshold. title: A forged member count in an aggregate snapshot kills the process unrecoverably (audit M-2)
description:
SECURITY AUDIT FINDING M-2 (plan/security-audit-phase-1.md), proved not theorised. This one is filed rather than carried because it BREAKS A RECORDED ARCHITECTURE DECISION.

THE BUG. internal/platform/snapcodec/set.go:136 does 'names := make([]string, 0, count)' where count is the blob's OWN uint32 claim, allocated BEFORE any check that the payload could hold that many members.

THE PROOF. A well-formed one-member container from the real SetWriter, count field overwritten to 0xFFFFFFFF, fed to OpenSet via a go test -overlay probe (nothing written into the tree) under ulimit -v 8000000: 'runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 68719476736-byte block ... fatal error: out of memory', frame snapcodec.OpenSet set.go:136. On a host with generous overcommit the same input instead commits 64 GB of address space and reads as a HANG.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SEVERITY SUGGESTS. This is a runtime THROW, not a panic -- NO recover() ANYWHERE CAN CATCH IT. So it bypasses both the httpx Recover middleware and the architecture rule in CLAUDE.md: 'Errors are values; a bad guest instruction halts visibly. It must never take the process down or, worse, continue plausibly.' A malformed snapshot currently takes the process down, which is the one outcome that decision forbids.

AND IT IS A SHARED PRIMITIVE. Every phase-4 restore path and every replay/oracle comparison inherits it. Today a snapshot is an operator-supplied file (SPEC FR-8) with no network ingress, which is why the audit rated it Medium rather than High -- but the input becomes less trusted the moment snapshots are exchanged, and the failure is total.

NOT A BUG NEXT DOOR: bus.decodeSnapshot (internal/bus/snapshot.go:179) gets this right -- it uses an unsized map. Reader.Words (snapcodec.go:362) also gets it right, checking remaining() first. OpenSet is the one that does not, which is why a single consistent guard is the fix rather than a style preference.

FIX (one line, plus its test): drop the capacity hint, or guard as Words does -- each member costs at least 8 bytes (two length prefixes), so refuse when uint64(count)*8 > uint64(r.remaining()), naming the claimed count and the bytes remaining. Add the forged-count case to set_test.go beside TestAHeaderCountThatDisagreesWithItsContentsIsRefused.

WATCH IT FAIL FIRST: reproduce the OOM with the forged count before fixing, then confirm the guard turns it into a named refusal. The phase rule applies -- the control must fire on an input the real system can actually produce, and a forged uint32 in a file is exactly that.

OWNER: p1-platform (snapcodec is its package).
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason:
Commit b02b06d. The finding is correct and the severity argument is right: this outranks its Medium rating because it breaks a recorded architecture decision, not merely because it crashes.

REPRODUCED BEFORE FIXING, from an input the real system can actually carry — a genuine one-member container with its count field overwritten to 0xFFFFFFFF, which is what a corrupt or hostile snapshot file contains. Built the probe through `go test -overlay` so the shared tree was never touched, and ran it under `ulimit -v 4000000`:

    runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 68719476736-byte block (3833856 in use)
    fatal error: out of memory
    runtime.throw(...)
    runtime.makeslice(...)
    snapcodec.OpenSet(...) set.go:136

A FORTY-BYTE BLOB. The stack confirms the lead's severity argument precisely: the frame is runtime.throw, not a panic, so no recover() anywhere can catch it — it goes past httpx.Recover and takes the process down. That is the one outcome "errors are values; a bad guest instruction halts visibly; it must never take the process down or, worse, continue plausibly" forbids. And on a host with generous overcommit it would not even fail loudly: it commits 64 GB of address space and reads as a hang.

THE FIX. Every member costs at least eight payload bytes — a four-byte length prefix for its name and another for its blob — so a container claiming more members than remaining/8 is describing a payload that is not there, and the claim is checked before anything is sized from it. The same forged blob now returns: "snapcodec: machine: snapshot blob is truncated: header claims 4294967295 members, which need at least 34359738360 payload bytes, and 15 remain". ErrTruncated is the honest sentinel: from the reader's side a forged count and a genuinely truncated blob are the same statement — the header claims more than is present.

The comparison widens to int64 rather than uint64, so both conversions are widening and cannot misrepresent their input. The largest product possible here (0xFFFFFFFF members at eight bytes, about 34 billion) fits int64 with room to spare, whereas an unsigned comparison would need remaining() proved non-negative first — a second thing to get right for no benefit. That also cleared a real gosec G115 finding rather than suppressing it.

THE GUARD SHADOWED ANOTHER ONE, and I caught it because this phase has now taught me to look. Two cases in TestAHeaderCountThatDisagreesWithItsContentsIsRefused previously surfaced as ErrShortRead and are now caught earlier by the count check; their expectations are updated, and — the important half — the short-read path gets a case of its OWN rather than being left unexercised behind the new check. It is still reachable whenever a plausible count contains a lying member length, so TestAMemberWhoseOwnLengthRunsOffTheEndIsRefused constructs exactly that: one member, enough bytes to be plausible, and a blob length pointing past the end. Without it, fixing this defect would have quietly retired a working guard — which is the same defect one level up.

PERMANENT CONTROLS ADDED, both firing on inputs the real system can produce: TestAForgedMemberCountIsRefusedBeforeAnythingIsAllocated does the byte-level overwrite of a real container (and asserts the error NAMES the claimed count and the writer, because "it returned an error" would also be satisfied by the reader running off the end a moment later — a different failure that looks the same from outside), and TestAMemberCountLargerThanThePayloadCouldHoldIsRefused covers the range including the boundary of one member too many.

MUTANT: removing the guard kills the suite by reproducing the original OOM at set.go:160 — run under a memory limit so that proving it could not thrash the host. A violent kill, but the right one: the mutant's failure IS the fault the guard prevents.

CHECKS: gofmt clean, go vet ./... exit 0, go test -race ./... exit 0 across 14 packages — including internal/bus, which consumes this container and whose own refusal tests pass unchanged — golangci-lint 0 issues, ./ctl.sh gate green. No probe file was left in the tree; it existed only as an overlay.

NOTED, NOT ACTIONED: M-1 (the loopback control being a default plus prose rather than an invariant) is carried onto gort-87m.2 as instructed and I have not touched it.

title: The boot gate's 'names the build' stage cannot fail for its stated reason
description:
FOUND BY THE LEAD while driving ./ctl.sh gate independently. The stage passes against exactly the binary it exists to reject, on every run.

THE EVIDENCE. A green run prints: 'ok  health names the build  version=dev commit=unknown'. 'dev' and 'unknown' are the LINKER DEFAULTS from internal/version -- they are what a binary reports when nobody told it what it is. That is the definition of unidentifiable, and the stage calls it ok.

WHY IT CANNOT FAIL. tools/boot-gate.sh:105 builds with a bare 'go build -o "/goretrotv" ./cmd/goretrotv' -- NO -ldflags, unlike the Makefile which injects Version/Commit/Date. So the binary under test can ONLY ever report dev/unknown. Line 170 then asserts merely '[[ -n "" && -n "" ]]' -- non-empty. Both placeholders are non-empty, so the assertion is satisfied by construction. The only route to a failure is the 'not reached' path, which is a different stage's failure wearing this stage's label.

THE NEGATIVE CONTROL FIRED ON A FAULT THE REAL SYSTEM CANNOT EXHIBIT. The stage WAS watched going red -- against a stub build returning an EMPTY version. But the real build path cannot produce an empty version; it produces 'dev'. So the control proved the assertion works on an input that will never occur, while the input that does occur passes. This is precisely the shape p1-qa was briefed to hunt: 'a negative control whose subject cannot actually exhibit the fault'.

WHY THE STAGE IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN DELETING. Its stated rationale is right and is the project's own: a gate that passes against a binary nobody can identify has proved nothing about the tree it was checking. The same defect was found and fixed EARLIER IN THIS PHASE in ctl.sh -- 'cmd_up' was letting compose default to VERSION=dev/COMMIT=unknown, and export_build_args was added precisely so /health would name the real build. The gate reintroduced it one layer down.

THE FIX:
1. Build with the same -ldflags the Makefile uses, so the binary under test carries a real version, commit and date. Reusing the Makefile's target is better than copying the flags: two definitions of the build identity is the duplication this project keeps paying for.
2. Assert IDENTIFIABILITY, not non-emptiness. The commit reported by /health should match the tree the gate is running against -- compare it to 'git rev-parse --short HEAD'. That is a claim that can actually be false.
3. WATCH IT FAIL ON THE REAL PATH: build without ldflags on purpose, confirm the stage goes red naming dev/unknown, then restore. A control that fires only on a synthetic input is the thing being fixed here, so the new control must fire on the input the system really produces.

OWNERSHIP: p1-platform -- tools/boot-gate.sh and ctl.sh are its files.
BLOCKS gort-6ar.17, which cannot honestly report the running stack verified while one of its stages is decorative.

close_reason:
Commit 23382d8. The finding is correct and the diagnosis was exact: the stage passed against precisely the binary it existed to reject, on every run.

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by reading rather than assumed: tools/boot-gate.sh built with a bare `go build` and no -ldflags, so the binary under test could only ever report the linker defaults from internal/version — `dev` and `unknown`. The assertion was `[[ -n "$version" && -n "$commit" ]]`. Both defaults are non-empty, so it was satisfied by construction, and the only route to red was the "not reached" path, which is a different stage's failure wearing this stage's label.

AND THE NEGATIVE CONTROL WAS THE REAL DEFECT. The stage WAS watched going red — against a stub returning an EMPTY version. The real build path cannot produce an empty version; it produces `dev`. So the control proved the assertion against a fault the system cannot exhibit, while the input that occurs on every single run passed. That is the exact shape p1-qa was briefed to hunt, and I built it into my own gate while writing negative controls for everything else.

FIX 1 — ONE DEFINITION OF THE BUILD IDENTITY. The gate now builds through the Makefile's own `build` target rather than re-implementing it. `build` gained a `BIN_DIR ?= bin` override, defaulting to bin/ so nothing changes for anyone else (verified: bare `make build` still writes goretrotv and oraclecmp to bin/), which lets the gate build into its scratch directory without a second copy of the ldflags existing anywhere. The duplication was the mechanism of the drift, not an incidental detail: the gate re-implemented the build and the re-implementation omitted the stamping.

FIX 2 — ASSERT IDENTITY, NOT NON-EMPTINESS. /health's commit must equal `git rev-parse --short HEAD`. That is a claim that can actually be false, and it is false the moment the stamping stops happening. It also answers the question that matters when a divergence turns up weeks later — was that binary built from this tree? — which is the same doubt that put oraclecmp in the image alongside the emulator. If HEAD cannot be determined at all the stage FAILS rather than passing, because an identity claim that cannot be checked is not granted.

WATCHED FAILING ON THE REAL PATH, which is the entire point of the fix rather than a formality:
- The real cmd/goretrotv, built exactly as the old gate built it (bare `go build`, no ldflags). This binary USED TO PASS this stage. It now fails it, ALONE — 1 of 5, with the other four stages green — which is what shows the stage is independently falsifiable rather than collapsing together with its neighbours. Message: "reports commit='unknown', this tree is 6e553e2 — those are the linker defaults, so the build was not stamped".
- A correctly stamped binary from a DIFFERENT commit: refused by name, "reports commit='da71a6e', this tree is 6e553e2". This is the version-skew case.
- A HALF-stamped binary (commit stamped to HEAD, version left at the default): refused as "half-stamped". I tested this branch specifically because it would otherwise have shipped unproven — the same dead-code-versus-missing-test discipline applied to my own fix.
- Control, the gate building for itself: green, "version=6e553e2-dirty commit=6e553e2 (matches HEAD)".

ALSO CORRECTED: the gate's own summary line said "The build does not come up" whatever had failed. That is false when the build came up and only the identity claim did not hold. It now reads "FAILED — N of 5 stages. Each FAIL line above says which claim did not hold." A gate's summary has to be as trustworthy as its stages, which is the same standard the stages are held to.

ON THE PATTERN, since the lead named it: this is the second time in the phase that a guard was satisfied by construction, and both times the tell was the same — the control fired on an input the system cannot produce. In snapcodec a surviving mutant meant unreachable code; in internal/oracle two survivors meant one floor shadowing another; here the control itself used a synthetic input. The generalisation is that watching an instrument fail is necessary but not sufficient: it must be watched failing on an input the real system can actually produce. I am recording that here rather than editing the shared library, which remains the lead's call with the user.

CHECKS: gofmt clean, go vet ./... exit 0, go test -race ./... exit 0 across 14 packages, golangci-lint 0 issues, bash -n clean on all three scripts, ./ctl.sh hooks green, ./ctl.sh gate green with all five stages. `make build` default behaviour verified unchanged. p1-core's in-flight cmd/oraclecmp/main.go and internal/platform/statehash/compare.go were verified absent from the staged set.

title: Pin the whole-machine hash across both emitters, and compare a real oracle stream to a Go stream
description:
TC-1.5 is ticked [x] with two limits recorded in plan/test-plan-phase-1.md. This issue closes them, and it BLOCKS gate gort-6ar.16 so the tick cannot outlive its caveats.

LIMIT 1 -- the drift guard pins the PRIMITIVES, not the composition. reference/digibox-boot.html:883-901: __cpVectors returns exactly mixWord_offset_80081C58, pageDigest_0_zeros and pageDigest_3_counting. There is NO whole-machine vector; 0x3D280665 (pinned on the Go side in statehash/vectors_test.go) has no counterpart in the page. So a field-order change or an ISA-encoding change inside cpHash() passes the oracle's self-test AND passes the committed agreement test. Both sides currently fold PC, ISA-as-octet, HI, LO, 32 GPR, 32 COP0 and the RAM digest in the same order -- verified BY READING, which is evidence of intent and not of behaviour.
FIX: add a whole-machine vector to __cpVectors and extend statehash/oracle_agreement_test.go to compare it.

LIMIT 2 -- oracle end-to-end determinism is a BY-HAND proof. Two cold boots agreed over a common window of 4,613 checkpoints (run2 a clean prefix of run1's 4,934), measured interactively via the Playwright MCP. Nothing committed re-runs it, so it cannot catch a regression.
FIX: once oraclecmp exists (gort-6ar.10), a committed check that compares a real oracle ?cp= stream against a Go stream. That is the artefact that makes TC-1.5's cross-implementation half reproducible instead of remembered.

WHY [x] AND NOT [?]: TC-1.5 as WRITTEN -- 'run the same program twice; then with the ISA bit flipped' -- is fully proved by committed Go tests (TestTwoIdenticalRunsProduceIdenticalStreams with a >=5-line vacuity guard; TestFlippingTheIsaBitDivergesTheStream asserting the FIRST differing line localises to the 3000 checkpoint). The emitter is committed (23487c1) and a committed cross-implementation guard exists (bc3feba), re-verified red by QA's own overlay. Marking that [?] would hide substantial committed proof; marking it [x] without recording the limits would overclaim. A tick with its scope written next to it, plus a tracked issue to close the scope, is the honest form of both.

A guard's SCOPE is part of its claim: 'the two implementations cannot drift silently' and 'their primitives cannot drift silently' are different promises, and only the second is built.

OWNERSHIP: p1-core (reference/digibox-boot.html, internal/platform/statehash, cmd/oraclecmp).

title: Re-point tools/check-digibox-boot.mjs at this repository, or retire it
description:
INHERITED AND STALE. tools/check-digibox-boot.mjs is the predecessor's boot gate, copied in with the project. p1-core enumerated exactly what is broken -- THREE things, not one:
- it resolves playwright through ../frontend/package.json; there is no frontend/ directory in this repo
- it reads the page from ../frontend/public/digibox-boot.html; ours is reference/digibox-boot.html
- it defaults to http://localhost:5173/digibox-boot.html; this project has no such route (8099 is the server port, and nothing serves the oracle yet)

So the file cannot run as it stands. Its header comments are excellent and record real measured failures (the batched device pumps that multiplied bootloaderHandoff's idle threshold by sixteen; the demux register file reading back its own writes and stopping the RTOS starting at all) -- that reasoning is worth keeping whatever happens to the code.

DECIDE, do not half-fix: either re-point all three and prove it runs against this repository, or retire it and move its recorded findings into docs/reference/. A half-fixed gate is worse than a visibly stale one, because a visibly stale gate is obviously not running while a half-fixed one looks live.

If re-pointed it must be PROVED RED: it ships a --self-test that deliberately breaks the machine and requires the section check to fail. Run that. A gate nobody has watched fail is decoration, and this one says so in its own header.

OWNERSHIP: belongs with TASK-1.11 (the ctl.sh boot gate) rather than with TASK-1.9. p1-core declined to fix it unasked, correctly -- 'half-fixing a stale gate is worse than leaving it visibly stale'.

Plus a specification of what a replacement harness must do.

A page with many calls and few definitions reaches one; a page with many definitions and NO calls reaches the other. That second case is the more dangerous, because if the call scan breaks there is nothing left to be undefined and the check reports a clean page having examined no calls at all — the vacuous green again. title: Migrate internal/bus/snapshot.go onto snapcodec.Set, removing the second set framing
description:
RULE 7 DEBT, CREATED KNOWINGLY, TO BE CLEARED THIS PHASE. Commit cbdadc1 added snapcodec.SetWriter/Set -- generic name-to-blob framing plus the completeness refusal. Verified just now: it has ZERO callers outside its own tests, while internal/bus/snapshot.go still does its own set framing on the low-level snapcodec.NewWriter/Open. That is two ways to frame a device set, both tested, both looking authoritative -- which is worse than either alone, because a future agent can reach for whichever they find first.

p1-platform built it and flagged the debt itself, asking to be held to the migration rather than letting it sit. This issue is that hold.

OWNERSHIP: p1-core. internal/bus/ is theirs and p1-platform must not edit it. Do it AFTER TASK-1.9 and TASK-1.10 -- the oracle chain is the delicate work and this is not urgent enough to interrupt it.

THE LINE, as p1-platform drew it and I have accepted:
- Generic and moves to snapcodec: the set FRAMING (name -> blob, versioned, counted, duplicate-rejecting, fully-consumed, name-ordered so equal sets encode to identical bytes) and the set-comparison REFUSAL (given an expected set of names, refuse and name what is missing and what is unexpected).
- Stays in bus: the POLICY that the expected set IS the attached devices. 'What is attached to this bus' is bus domain knowledge and CLAUDE.md is explicit that domain knowledge stays in its package.

VERIFICATION: the migration is a refactor with the tests already written. TestRestoreRefusesASnapshotMissingADevice and TestRestoreRefusesASnapshotNamingADeviceThatIsNotThere must still pass UNCHANGED -- if they need editing to accommodate the move, the move changed behaviour and that needs saying out loud. Byte-identical encoding for equal sets must survive (FR-7 compares snapshots, it does not only restore them). And bustest.CheckSnapshot must still fail the deliberately-forgetful device.

WHY NOT DEFER TO PHASE 4: phase 4 (gort-lbl) is where the second caller appears -- the machine snapshot over bus + cpu + clock -- which is the honest trigger for extracting an abstraction. But deferring means shipping phase 1 with a known parallel implementation, gate gort-6ar.18 would flag it as drift, and 'we will unify it later' is how two authoritative formats become permanent.

title: Promote the single-module assertion from a CI step to a conformance rule
description:
TASK-1.4 (commit b23052b) added a CI step asserting the module graph holds exactly ONE module, guarding ADR 0001's zero-dependency decision. It belongs in the conformance estate rather than as a loose workflow step -- p1-platform said so when building it and offered it as a two-line move.

WHY IT IS WORTH A RULE. ADR 0001 states no-dependencies is a FLOOR, NOT A VOW: a later phase that genuinely needs a dependency (the WebSocket transport in phase 5, ffmpeg for Video) should take one. What must not happen is erosion -- somebody running 'go get' and nobody noticing. A conformance rule makes taking a dependency a DELIBERATE edit to the rule rather than an unremarked change to go.mod, which is exactly the distinction /architecture-conformance exists to enforce.

Pairs with ARCH-LAYER-1 (internal/platform importing nothing outward), which is already in this epic's scope. Same shape: a recorded decision that nothing currently enforces.

REQUIRED: the probe must be watched failing -- add a dependency on a scratch branch, see the rule go red, remove it. A conformance rule that has never rejected anything is decoration, and this epic's whole purpose is rules that can still fail.

title: Wire firmware.Load into the startup path so a mismatch refuses the boot
description:
TC-1.4 says 'refuses to START, naming the mismatch'. The loader refuses correctly and is proved at package level (TASK-1.7), but NOTHING CALLS IT: grep confirms firmware.Load appears only in its own tests, and neither cmd/goretrotv nor internal/app references the package. So half of TC-1.4 -- the half the test case actually names -- is unwired, and the phase would have closed with a loader nobody invokes.

Two gaps that are really one:
1. No startup path calls firmware.Load, so a checksum mismatch cannot refuse a boot that never consults it.
2. GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR does not exist in internal/config. p1-core correctly declined to add a config field nothing reads, and nothing reads it because nothing calls Load. Adding both together is what makes either coherent.

SCOPE:
- Add GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR to internal/config. Decide REQUIRED vs defaulted deliberately and state the reasoning: the test to apply is the one used for GORETROTV_ENV -- if a wrong guess means silently running a different ROM, it is required. The completeness test will force it into the committed example file.
- Call firmware.Load on the startup path so a mismatch, a missing image or a wrong size EXITS NON-ZERO naming the problem, before anything else initialises.
- This also closes the latent container trap: the image mounts firmware at /firmware while a relative firmware/ path works only because distroless sets no WORKDIR. Anything that later sets one turns this into a wrong-or-absent ROM, which is TC-1.4's own subject arriving through the back door.

PROOF (this is an instrument; watch it fail):
- Built binary, real firmware present -> starts.
- Built binary, one image corrupted -> exits non-zero naming the file and the digest mismatch.
- Built binary, firmware dir absent/empty -> exits non-zero naming what is missing.
- Assert the OUTCOME, not the absence of an exception: confirm the process did NOT reach 'listening'.

OWNERSHIP: p1-platform owns internal/config, internal/app and cmd/goretrotv. p1-core owns internal/firmware and must not edit those files. p1-core raised this rather than quietly widening scope into another agent's file, which is the correct call and why this is its own issue rather than a silent edit.

DECISION — GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR is REQUIRED, and the reasoning is sharper than the GORETROTV_ENV case rather than merely analogous. firmware.Load reads MANIFEST.md from the SAME directory it is pointed at and verifies the images against it, so the checksum guard structurally cannot notice a wrong DIRECTORY: a different firmware set arrives with its own manifest and verifies perfectly against itself. - one image missing -> exit 1, naming the file. Never reached listening.
- firmware directory absent -> exit 1, naming the manifest path. Never reached listening.
- firmware directory present but empty -> exit 1, naming the manifest path. Never reached listening.
- GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR unset -> exit 1, "missing required environment variable: GORETROTV_FIRMWARE_DIR (see the example env file)". Never reached listening.

And per the lead's driver-reaches-subject rule, the config walk now asserts it reached EVERY field of the struct rather than at least five -- watched failing with a mutant that adds a field the walk cannot see, which the old MustFind(>=5) accepted at six-of-seven and the new check rejects by name with the count of fields it never reached.

to find for the grid: it enters the listings module 0x800A8000..0x800AB000 ZERO times while it
draws. It does not ask and get nothing. IT NEVER ASKS. The decision is a branch in interpreted

HOW IT WAS READ. tools/ocode-disasm.py has existed and been validated for a while and had never
been pointed at this port, because its only trace producer was a browser probe against the
oracle. The interpreter fetches bytecode from FLASH AS DATA, so every flash read is an o-code
program counter; internal/multiplex/firmwaretests/ocodetrace_firmware_test.go now writes
.artifacts/grid-ocode-trace.csv in the pc,address,size,icount format the tool wants (177,375

THE CONDITION:

  9fc7390c  push_fp_minus16
  9fc7390d  push_ds
  9fc7390e  add_nnnnnnnn 0x0002e250      ; ds + 0x2E250 + 336*row
  9fc73913  add

  9fc73917  push_2

segment. Measured: records at 0x8048ADB4 + 336*n, all six holding 1, ds = 0x8045CB64.

title: [TASK-6.8] Re-read the schedule file while running; a malformed edit keeps the last good line-up and

Semantic faults (a duplicate listingsId, which parses and would broadcast plausibly wrong) are refused the same way as unparseable ones.
