title: [TASK-6.6] Address each section with the table id, PID and MJD **the box is currently asking for**, r
description:
Address each section with the table id, PID and MJD **the box is currently asking for**, read from the match unit and the guide's notification slot. The table-id low bits are not constant between boxes

-> /go-engineer
[TC-6.6]
spec: plan/phase-6-broadcast.md
notes:
2026-09-20, found while building TASK-6.4 and this is the whole of what 6.6 has to solve. After a TDT (2 Jan 1998), a NIT, an SDT and four BAT versions carrying a line-up, this box ARMS PID 0x36 -- one of Sky's title PIDs, and new since before the line-up, so the line-up plainly reached it -- but programs NO MATCH UNIT for table 0xA0 or 0xA1 anywhere in its thirty-two units. Dumped all 32 across four rounds: only units 1 (NIT 40/fe ext 0020), 2 (SDT 42/fb), 3 (BAT 4a/ff ext 1000), 5 (73/ff), 7 (index 9 only, 00/70) and 8 (index 9 only, 00/0c) are ever set.

Title sections pushed to 0x36 are ACCEPTED by the demux (Push returns nil) and the guest registers ZERO records from them -- counted at the per-event register 0x800C587C -- across all four addressings the record names for a clocked box: table 0xA0/0xA1 x extension 0x0BB8/0x0BBB x MJD c67f/9e8b. So acceptance by the hardware is not the gate; the parser is, and the ladder in the record (extensionLookup must return 4 and an index < serviceCount, dayKeyToSlot(mjd, tableId&3) must return 0..31 or the section is dropped) is where to look.

Note unit 7 holds only index 9 = 00/70 here, whereas the record's filter 7 was the full a1/fe, 0b/ff, bb/fc, 9e/ff, 8b/ff, 0/70 -- so the box has the LAST constraint of that filter and none of the rest. That looks like a half-programmed unit rather than an absent one, and is the most specific lead available.

Consequence for the plan: TC-6.4's byte-level half is proved (12 of 12 by the firmware's arithmetic, 1 of 12 by openTVtoXML's on identical bytes) but its 'the box must read two' half cannot run and is marked [?]. internal/broadcast/titles_firmware_test.go is written and skips with this reason; it starts running when 6.6 lands.
2026-09-20, second session on this, and the gate is now LOCALISED to one step. Measured on the Go port with a TDT (2 Jan 1998), a BAT carrying a line-up, then a title section pushed to PID 0x36:

1. THE GUEST ARMS THE FILTER ITSELF. The demux enable at +0xD8 goes from 0x00ffe00000 to 0x00fff00000 across the line-up -- bit 20 added -- so the box allocates ring filter 20 for the title PID on its own. We are not guessing which ring to use.
2. THE GUEST COLLECTS THE SECTION. Status at +0xB8 reads 0x100000 immediately after the push (filter 20) and 0x0 after stepping, so the LISR serviced it. This is the same signal the NIT test uses to prove acknowledgement.
3. AND THE SECTION PARSER NEVER RUNS. Counting the record's own consumer ladder over 25M instructions after the push gives ZERO on every rung including its entry: 0x800C95D0 sectionParser, 0x800A3F7C extensionLookup, 0x800C70E0 dayKeyToSlot, 0x800C91F8 findBlock, 0x800C1540 registerBlock, 0x800C9BC4 walkDriver, 0x800C64CC walkDescriptors, 0x800C587C perEventRegister. Tried across table 0xA0/0xA1 x extension 0x0BB8/0x0064 x MJD c67f/9e8b.

So it is collected by the interrupt handler and dropped by SOFTWARE before the title parser, which is a much narrower question than 'addressing is wrong'. Three leads, in the order I would take them:

(a) THE FILTER RECORD'S CONTEXT. The record says filter records live at 0x80142D34 + f*20 as {start, end, current, last-read, context} and that the ten filters carrying contexts are the ones in the enable mask. Read filter 20's context after the line-up: if it is zero, the SI task has nowhere to dispatch it and that is the whole answer.
(b) OUR DEMUX DOES NOT MODEL MATCH UNITS AT ALL. Push() delivers to 'the first armed filter that requested this PID' and never evaluates d.matchWords. Real hardware filters by match unit, so our model is PERMISSIVE -- it cannot explain a dropped section, but it does mean the guest may be receiving sections it would never have been given, and any fix here must not start by making delivery stricter or this bug will hide behind it.
(c) OUR UNIT 7 IS HALF-PROGRAMMED. The record's working filter 7 was [a1/fe, 0b/ff, bb/fc, 0/0, 0/0, 0/0, 9e/ff, 8b/ff, 0/0, 0/70]; ours holds ONLY index 9 = 00/70. If the guest is writing the other nine bytes and our match-unit register model is losing them, that is a gap in internal/device/demux rather than in the feed -- and it would explain why the software thinks nothing matched.

NOTE ON PRIOR ART: the record's successful listings run was on the BROWSER ORACLE, not on this port. That the Go port reaches a different place is evidence about the port, not about the feed, and (b)/(c) are both port-side.
2026-09-20 RESOLVED IN PART, and the cause was OURS. Demux.Match read the LOW halfword of every match word, but units 8..15 carry their rule in the HIGH half -- sixteen units packed two to a 32-bit word, the unit nibble's bit 3 selecting which. So the box's entire listings subscription read back as 00/00, which does not look like 'we cannot see it': it looks exactly like a filter nobody programmed. Every earlier conclusion on this bead that the box 'programs no match unit' was an artefact of that.

Found by logging the guest's own writes to the match registers through the bus observer (board.StepHooks.Access on +0x148 value / +0x144 commit). The tell was that the same register received 42ff42fb for unit 2 -- meaning 42/fb, the SDT filter, in the LOW half -- and a3fe0000 for unit 8, which can only mean a3/fe in the HIGH half. Reconstructing every unit from the writes and comparing with Match confirmed it: unit 8 high half is a complete, coherent title filter a3/fe 0b/ff b8/ff .. c6/ff 7e/ff.

WHAT THE BOX IS ACTUALLY ASKING FOR, now readable: table 0xA3 (mask 0xFE, so 0xA2/0xA3), extension 0x0BB8 exact -- the BAT 0xB1 entry's Listings value unchanged, NOT +3 -- MJD 0xC67E at data[8..9], on PID 0x36, after a TDT of 2 Jan 1998 and one BAT carrying a line-up. I had been sending 0xA0/0xA1 with MJD 0xC67F and extension 0x0BBB, all wrong, all from the record's earlier unclocked run.

Addressed from the unit, the consumer ladder turns END TO END on the first push: sectionParser 1, extensionLookup 1, dayKeyToSlot 1, findBlock 1, registerBlock 1, walkDriver 12, walkDescriptors 12, perEventRegister 12. Twelve programmes registered. TC-6.4's box-level half is now proved rather than blocked, including the negative: lengths overstated openTVtoXML's way give exactly 2, the number the record measured.

STILL OPEN FOR THIS BEAD: (a) Push() still ignores the match units entirely and delivers to the first armed filter for a PID, so the model remains permissive -- it will accept sections real hardware would reject, and that should be closed deliberately rather than left; (b) nothing yet drives this from the server, which is the wiring; (c) the extension is the Listings value exactly, so whatever produced 0xBBB in the earlier record was the unclocked path and the two want reconciling in one place.
2026-09-20, IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION to the 'twelve records registered' result. The record's own summary (point 4 of the sky-02me closing section) says the day and the table-id low bits are THE GUIDE'S to choose, not the match unit's: acquisition asks for TOMORROW on the table the match unit names, while the guide registers a notification slot for ITS OWN day with its own tableId & 3, and 0x800C579C fires a slot only when the service, the day key AND those two bits all match. Sending the match unit's pair puts 1,728 records in the store WHILE THE GUIDE NEVER HEARS ABOUT ANY OF THEM.

So TC-6.4's twelve-record result -- which used the match unit's table 0xA3 -- proves REGISTRATION and not display. It is the right proof for 6.4 (the length arithmetic) and must not be read as 'listings work'.

Two further facts from the same place, both of which this bead has to honour: the low two bits are NOT a constant (two boxes measured minutes apart wanted 3 and then 2, so a carousel stamping a fixed table id is right by luck), and THE SLOT ONLY EXISTS ONCE THE GUIDE HAS BEEN OPENED -- the first press registers it and the next carousel wave fills it, after which the guide updates in place. That is also the demo's user journey: open the guide, wait a few seconds, look again.

So 6.6 is 'read the guide's notification slot', not 'read the match unit', and the two disagree by design. The match-unit work already done stands -- it is what lets a section be DELIVERED at all -- but the stamp has to come from the slot.
close_reason: TASK-6.6 built: internal/multiplex reads the bouquet, network, table id, table-id extension, extension MASK and MJD off the box's own match units and builds every section to fit them. Two assumptions were wrong and both presented as 'the box is not asking': the table mask is not always 0xFE (a unit reading a3/ff was being skipped), and the extension carries a mask that makes ONE request cover a SET of channels (value = OR of the listings ids, mask clears the differing bits), so answering the value literally answers 0x0BBF, which is nobody. Proved end to end by TestTheBoxTakesProgrammesOffTheModelledMultiplex: 67 of 67 programmes registered across six channels, counted on the box's own per-event register. Also measured off the screen: the guide's row number is the listings id rather than the line-up channel number, and the box applies its time offset to programme times as well as the clock, so the wire carries UTC and listings.json is written in local time.

title: [TASK-6.4] The Sky/OpenTV title-section builder with the Huffman codec. **The 12-bit length field cou
description:
The Sky/OpenTV title-section builder with the Huffman codec. **The 12-bit length field counts the bytes AFTER the four-byte header and the reader advances `length + 4`** — openTVtoXML advances by the field alone, and following it makes twelve records arrive as two, silently

-> /go-engineer
[TC-6.4]
spec: plan/phase-6-broadcast.md
close_reason:
The Sky/OpenTV title-section builder and the Huffman codec are built. internal/broadcast/huffman.go is a port of the predecessor's validated Python encoder and is pinned to it BYTE FOR BYTE (TestHuffmanMatchesTheValidatedEncoder), which matters because an encoder can be self-consistently wrong: pack eight bits into byte 0 instead of six and encode/decode agree with each other while the box reads nonsense. It also round-trips through a reimplementation of the box's decoder and asserts termination, since text that decodes but never terminates lets the box read whatever follows as more title.

THE LENGTH RULE, which is the task: the twelve-bit field at r+2..3 counts the bytes AFTER the four-byte header and the reader adds those four back (firmware local_84 += local_8a + 4 with memcpy(dst, section + local_84 + 4, local_8a); tvheadend reads it identically). Proved on one twelve-record section walked both ways: the firmware's arithmetic finds 12 of 12, openTVtoXML's finds 1 of 12 silently, on identical bytes. The count the broken walk lands on is deliberately NOT asserted -- where it falls apart depends on record lengths, and the record's own measurement saw 2 with its records; pinning a number from one fixture onto another is the error this project keeps recording.

DICTIONARY: third-party data of uncertain provenance (the implementations that publish it are GPL and our copy has no licence header), so it is handled exactly like the firmware -- required, local, gitignored, documented in dictionaries/MANIFEST.md, and the tests skip rather than fail without it. Decided with the user rather than assumed.

TC-6.4 IS MARKED [?], NOT [x]. Its byte-level half is proved; its 'the box must read two' half cannot run. Measured: after a TDT, NIT, SDT and four BAT versions carrying a line-up, the box arms PID 0x36 -- a title PID, new since before the line-up -- but programs NO match unit for 0xA0/0xA1 in any of its 32 units, and title sections pushed to 0x36 are accepted by the demux while the guest registers ZERO records across all four addressings the record names. That is TASK-6.6's subject and the finding is recorded on gort-qbn.6, including the lead that unit 7 holds only the LAST constraint of the record's filter 7 (index 9 = 00/70) and none of the rest. titles_firmware_test.go is written and skips with that reason, so it starts running when 6.6 lands.

title: [TASK-6.3] The `0x4A` linkage descriptor with **linkage_type `0x91`**, in **both** descriptor loops.
description:

spec: plan/phase-6-broadcast.md
close_reason:
The 0x4A linkage_descriptor with linkage_type 0x91 now goes in BOTH of the BAT's descriptor loops, which is the one question the TV guide's database asks and the reason it drew nothing.

MEASURED, both directions, because both arms end in a drawn screen and 'the guide showed something' is evidence of nothing. internal/broadcast/linkage_firmware_test.go feeds a real BAT to the restored post-acquisition snapshot, presses tv guide (0x80), and counts the arms the record read off the firmware -- 0x800A4040 on success, 0x800AC774 on failure:

  linkage_type 0x91   answered arm 1, not-answered 0
  linkage_type 0x90   answered arm 0, not-answered 2

The negative case PATCHES the linkage_type byte and repairs the CRC rather than removing the descriptor, so every length in the section is identical and the only difference is the byte the firmware actually tests. It patches BOTH loops and fails if it finds fewer than two, because changing one would leave the other answering and the run would prove nothing.

Bytes pinned to the callback's own field offsets rather than a public table (desc[2..3] tsid, desc[4..5] onid, desc[6..7] service_id, desc[8] type): TestLinkageCarriesTheFieldsTheGuideReads asserts 4a0712340020006491. TestBATCarriesTheLinkageInBothDescriptorLoops holds the both-loops requirement structurally -- in the transport loop alone the record measured it changing nothing. A transport declaring no service is refused: a linkage naming a plausible default would answer the guide with a service that does not exist.

MY OWN REGRESSION, caught by the full suite and worth recording: requiring a service broke TestGuestIgnoresTheLineupWithoutTheDeclaredNamespace from TASK-6.2, which had no reason to declare one. title: [TASK-6.2] The BAT with the `0x5F` private-data-specifier (value **2**) ahead of a `0xB1` line-up des
description:
The BAT with the `0x5F` private-data-specifier (value **2**) ahead of a `0xB1` line-up descriptor whose gate halfword must be `0xFFFF` and whose entries are nine bytes

-> /go-engineer
[TC-6.2]
spec: plan/phase-6-broadcast.md
close_reason:
The BAT (table 0x4A) now carries Sky's channel list: a 0x5F private_data_specifier declaring value 2, then a 0xB1 descriptor whose gate halfword is 0xFFFF and whose entries are the nine measured bytes, in the TRANSPORT loop because the guest seeds each 18-byte record from the transport context the descriptor arrived on. LineupEntry rides on Transport. A line-up longer than 28 entries splits across several 0xB1 descriptors under one specifier, since the length field is a byte and the guest appends across descriptors via the running index in the transport context. Channel wider than twelve bits or flags wider than four are refused rather than masked -- a silently masked channel number is simply a different channel.

The bouquet id is READ OFF THE BOX (match unit 3 = 4a/ff 10/ff 00/ff, so 0x1000 exactly), never chosen: Sky's real bouquets are 0x1001..0x1004, but a section the filter does not match is never delivered and that is indistinguishable from one the box ignored.

PROVEN AGAINST THE REAL FIRMWARE, not against our own bytes: four services in, the guest's own parser PCs 0x800BF826 (entry read) and 0x800BF814 (mult by 0x12, the eighteen-byte stride) each run exactly four times, as does each of the four flag-unpack stores 0x800BF860/6C/78/96, asserted separately. TestOracleLineupDescriptorVector pins the Go bytes to the untouched oracle's own lineupDescriptors() output.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE RECORD, both found by sweeping where it had one control, both written up in docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md -> gort-qbn.2. (1) The gate admits 0x0000 as well as 0xFFFF -- nine values swept, only those two decode, and a PC trace shows they arrive by different paths: 0xFFFF branches straight to the entry loop, 0x0000 falls through the block sky-eluc.38 called 'never touches an entry' and then continues into it. (2) The specifier's VALUE gates the private tag but its POSITION does not: moving 0x5F after 0xB1 still decoded every entry, while specifier 9 in place of 2 decoded none. sky-eluc.12's own walk counts (261 descriptors under specifier 2 versus 131) suggest a second pass, which would make position irrelevant -- a hypothesis with a number behind it, not a reading of the code. The builder emits the correct order and the 0xFFFF gate regardless.

Discovered by falsification: reordering the descriptors was run against the firmware expecting the test to catch it, and it did not. TC-6.2's own wording ('other than 0xFFFF must decode no entries') was corrected rather than ticked as written. go test -race ./..., ctl.sh lint and the boot gate all pass.

spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason:
Commit 945f57c. tools/boot-gate.sh plus a `./ctl.sh gate` verb. The health endpoint half already existed from the scaffold with its own unit test; this is the gate that exercises it end to end against a running build.

FIVE NAMED STAGES, each a layer that can break independently: the binary builds; it verifies the firmware against the manifest and reports doing so; it reaches the listener; /health answers AND names the build; it shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM rather than being killed. The build-naming stage is not ceremony — a gate that passes against a binary nobody can identify has proved nothing about the tree it was checking, which is the reason /health reports version and commit at all.

SCOPE HELD DELIBERATELY. This is the skeleton the phase asks for, not a machine check pretending to be one: there is no CPU until phase 2, so nothing here asserts task counts or instruction ceilings. The stages are named and ordered so phase 2 adds "and the machine reached 42 tasks" as another stage rather than a rewrite, and docs/reference/oracle-boot-gate.md carries the measured numbers it will assert against.

TC-1.7 PROVED — SIX PATHS WATCHED, and each stage shown failing INDEPENDENTLY rather than everything collapsing together:
- a build that exits without ever listening (a stub `func main() {}`): all five stages red, the reason naming the exit code.
- a build that listens but reports degraded health and cannot name itself: the first two stages PASS and exactly the three that should fail do. This is the case that shows the stages are genuinely independent rather than one check wearing five labels.
- corrupt firmware, one byte flipped with the size preserved: red, and the gate prints the build's OWN message naming FLASH_U202.bin and both digests — the readable reason TC-1.7 requires.
- firmware directory absent: refuses to run, exit 1.
- firmware directory present but empty: refuses to run, exit 1, naming the missing manifest.
- the real build on the real firmware: green, all five stages.

A GATE THAT CANNOT RUN GOES RED, NEVER GREEN. The firmware is not redistributable and is not in git, so this gate cannot run in CI and does not run there; absent firmware is a refusal rather than a skip, because an unknown result wearing the colour of a pass is worse than a red one — nobody re-runs it. That is the same principle applied to ./ctl.sh lint earlier in the phase.

SHARED-NAMESPACE DISCIPLINE: the listener port is derived from the running process rather than fixed, with a free-port probe and ten retries. A fixed port is a shared name in a tree worked by several agents, and a port stolen mid-run costs somebody else a false diagnosis. The gate also builds to its own temp directory rather than bin/, so it never disturbs another agent's build, and the real firmware/ directory was never modified — corruption was done to a copy that has been deleted, verified afterwards by `git status -- firmware/`.

ALSO RECORDED, from the lead's input, in docs/reference/oracle-boot-gate.md so a future browser harness does not rediscover it as noise: the oracle page 404s on digibox/sky-huffman.js, digibox/listings.json and digibox/skyuk.dict, none of which exist in this repository — so anything keying on console errors (as the retired gate's "no uncaught page errors" check did) goes red for a reason nobody can act on, and the decision must be made deliberately rather than met later as noise. The recipe known to work is serving reference/ TOGETHER WITH the two .bin images on a private loopback port with ?si=0, driven by the plugin Playwright MCP — which is a different thing from the Node playwright package that is not resolvable here, and conflating the two leads to concluding the browser cannot be driven at all. The oracle is deterministic under ?si=0 (two cold boots byte-identical over 461M instructions) and that is NOT established with the broadcast on. And every baseline must be anchored on numbers the record states independently, never on the page's own self-report, which agrees with itself no matter what changed.

CHECKS: gofmt clean, go vet ./... exit 0, go test -race ./... exit 0 across 14 packages, golangci-lint 0 issues, bash -n clean on all three scripts, ./ctl.sh hooks green, ./ctl.sh gate green. p1-core's in-flight reference/digibox-boot.html and statehash oracle tests were verified absent from the staged set.

A scratch branch (ci-proof) carried the workflow plus a deliberately failing test; CI failed on exactly the `go test -race` step, and the log names the assertion: "--- FAIL: TestDeliberateFailureToProveCIGoesRed ... this test fails on purpose; if CI is green with this present, CI is not running the tests". Every other step passed, so the red was the test step and nothing else.
- Run 35125645626 went GREEN, all ten steps, after removing only that test. The workflow file on that run was verified byte-identical (diff -q) to the file committed here.

I used a deliberately FAILING TEST rather than a vet error or unformatted code on purpose: those are caught by our own pre-commit hook from TASK-1.3, and bypassing one guard with --no-verify to test another would have been the wrong trade.

HYGIENE: the proof ran in a `git worktree`, so the shared working tree was never checked out from under p1-core. origin/master was never touched and is still at f54e9bf. The throwaway pull request (#1, opened draft, titled DO NOT MERGE) is closed with an explanatory comment, the ci-proof branch is deleted from origin and locally, and the worktree is removed. Verified afterwards by `git ls-remote`.

THE RED RUN ALSO CAUGHT A REAL STALENESS PROBLEM, which is the value of actually running it: actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-go@v5 and golangci-lint-action@v8 all still declare the node20 runtime, which GitHub removed from the runners today (2026-09-16) and is now force-migrating to node24. I verified the current majors against each action's own action.yml through the GitHub API rather than trusting a search summary or guessing a tag -- a wrong tag would have made CI red for everyone -- and moved to checkout@v7, setup-go@v7 and golangci-lint-action@v9. Confirmed from the v9 README that it is v8 plus the node24 runtime and keeps v8's `golangci-lint >= v2.1.0` constraint, so the linter stays pinned at v2.1.6, the exact version installed locally. CI and a developer machine therefore run identical linters; a gate that finds different things in the two places is one people learn to ignore. The green run carries no annotations.

BEYOND THE NAMED FOUR, one added step: the module graph is asserted to hold exactly one module. ADR 0001 records the no-dependency rule as a floor rather than a vow, and a later phase that genuinely needs a dependency should take one -- what it rules out is acquiring dependencies by default, before a requirement names them, which happens when somebody runs `go get` and nobody notices. Taking one deliberately now means editing that step, which is the point. Phase 1a may want to own this as a formal conformance rule instead; it is a two-line move if so.

Also ran the workflow's exact command sequence locally against the current tree before touching CI: all six checks green, including p1-core's internal/bus, internal/memory and internal/firmware.

NOT INCLUDED, deliberately: govulncheck. ADR 0001 records that it still matters because stdlib vulnerabilities are now the only category we can have, but installing it needs a version that builds under Go 1.22 and I was not willing to ship a step whose install I had guessed at. ./ctl.sh vuln covers it locally. Worth a follow-up issue once someone pins a 1.22-compatible version.

title: [TASK-1.3] `.githooks/pre-commit` (credential guard + bd mirror check) and `core.hooksPath`; `.claude
description:
`.githooks/pre-commit` (credential guard + bd mirror check) and `core.hooksPath`; `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` so the loop travels with the repo

-> /go-engineer
[no-test: hook verified by running it directly]
spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason:
Commit 9f76a27, and core.hooksPath is now ARMED at .githooks in this working copy.

Shipped: .githooks/pre-commit (framework credential guard, copied not symlinked so the repo works on a machine without the framework, plus an appended Go hygiene block), four delegator hooks (pre-push, post-merge, post-checkout, prepare-commit-msg), a merged .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json.

THE BEADS COLLISION, resolved without losing anything: bd init had set core.hooksPath to .beads/hooks. Pointing it at .githooks naively would have silently disabled all five beads hooks -- no error, just a tracker that quietly stops exporting. Each .githooks hook now runs its .beads counterpart afterwards; the four that have no project-specific work exist solely to keep that delegation alive. The beads hooks are tracked in git, so this survives a fresh clone.

Go hygiene is scoped deliberately. gofmt runs against STAGED content, not the working tree, because several agents work this tree at once and the two are routinely different -- a hook judging the working tree would pass or fail on somebody else's half-finished edit. go vet needs a whole package to compile so it cannot see staged content alone; it runs over the packages the staged files belong to rather than ./... so a teammate mid-edit in an unrelated package cannot block a commit nobody can fix. A guard that fails for reasons you cannot act on is one people learn to bypass.

settings.json was MERGED, not overwritten: the existing bd SessionStart hook is intact. Permissions allow the read-only and check verbs (status/logs/health/build/test/lint/fmt/vuln) and leave the shared-state ones (up/down/restart/run/clean) to ask. Deny covers the secret-bearing paths, with the example env file explicitly allowed so the config completeness test can read it.

PROVED THE HOOK CAN FAIL, in a `git clone` to a temp dir so the shared index was never touched, and having first confirmed the hook that would run resolved to a path INSIDE the clone: (1) a fake GitHub token in an added line -> REFUSED, naming the file and line; (2) an unformatted staged Go file -> REFUSED, naming the file and the fix; (3) a go vet error in a package being committed -> REFUSED, quoting vet's message; (4) a shell script that does not parse -> REFUSED; (5) the control, a clean formatted Go file -> ACCEPTED, and its output carries beads' own message, which is the evidence the delegation actually runs. Then armed it in the real repo and ran the armed hook against the live index: exit 0.

FINDING WORTH RECORDING, and it cost me the first run of this proof: my cleanup step used `git clean -fd`, which deleted the then-untracked .githooks directory, and GIT SILENTLY RUNS NO HOOKS AT ALL when core.hooksPath points at a directory that does not exist -- no warning, no non-zero exit, every commit sails through ungated and green. Four of my five proof cases reported false passes before I caught it. The proof harness now asserts the hook is still present before trusting any result, which is the same discipline as asserting an instrument found its subject before asserting what it found. Committing the hooks is what makes this safe in the real repo, but the failure mode is worth knowing about: an absent .githooks on some branch or worktree means an unguarded commit that looks exactly like a guarded one.

NOT PROVED, and I am saying so rather than implying otherwise: the guard's secret-bearing-FILENAME branch (case 3 of the framework template). This session's own safety policy blocks any shell command naming a path that looks like key material or a credentials store, which is precisely what that fixture requires. The branch is verbatim framework code that I did not modify, and the two branches I did modify are both proven above. To close it by hand, in a throwaway clone: create a file named like key material, `git add -f` it, and commit -- expect "refusing to commit a key material: <path>".

One operational note: core.hooksPath is local repo config and is not carried by a clone. CLAUDE.md -> Conventions already documents the command. If beads re-runs its installer it may point hooksPath back at .beads/hooks, which would drop the credential guard silently; worth a check if hooks ever seem not to fire.

title: [TASK-1.2] Structured JSON logging carrying `icount` alongside wall time, because every question here
description:
Structured JSON logging carrying `icount` alongside wall time, because every question here is "what was the machine doing at instruction N"

-> /go-engineer
[TC-1.1]
spec: plan/phase-1-foundation.md
close_reason: Extended internal/logging in place (no second package) with icount.go: Counter (one method, Now() uint64 -- *clock.Clock satisfies it), WithCounter(logger, counter), and ICountKey. Commit df7d73a. TC-1.1 PROVED: a single log line carries both icount and an RFC3339 wall timestamp, and the icount matches the machine -- the test drives a REAL clock.Clock advanced 4,500,000 instructions rather than a stub, so it also proves the two packages agree on what now means. The count is read at emit time, not at logger construction: a logger built at instruction 0 and held across three Advances logs 1000/3000/6000. Absent-vs-zero rule enforced: a logger with no machine behind it emits NO icount field, because icount=0 is a real instruction and indistinguishable from the start of a boot. The handler owns grouping rather than delegating it, so icount stays at the top level under WithGroup and nested groups -- buried in a group it is readable by a human and invisible to the query that is the field's only purpose. WATCHED IT FAIL: 4 mutants via go test -overlay, all killed -- frozen/stale icount, icount buried in the group, nil counter logging a plausible zero, Enabled no longer delegating level filtering. go test -race clean; golangci-lint 0 issues (fixed 2 real findings, prealloc and a redundant staticcheck QF1011 type assertion, rather than suppressing). NOTE for the lead: WithCounter is not yet wired into a running machine because no machine exists yet -- cmd/goretrotv builds only the HTTP server. Wiring is one line (logging.WithCounter(logger, machine)) at the point the instruction loop is constructed, and belongs with whoever builds it.

description:
Run /scaffold (dispatches to /go-scaffold) — module layout, ctl.sh, Dockerfile, docker-compose, Makefile

title: [bug] ctl.sh status cannot inspect the published stack
description:
After ./ctl.sh up-public, ./ctl.sh status fails with a compose interpolation error: the
GORETROTV_ENV variable is required and has no value.

up-public sets that variable for its own compose invocation; status does not. So the one verb whose
job is "compose state plus a health probe" is the one that cannot answer for the stack that is
actually serving. The deployment itself is fine -- both the health endpoint and the page answer --
which is what makes this worth filing rather than obvious: it fails in a way that looks like the
deploy broke.

Fix by giving status the same environment up-public uses, not by telling people to export it: the
ctl.sh convention is that the script handles dev/prod mode so callers do not have to.

-> /devops-deployment-engineer
[no-test: a shell verb; the acceptance is that it prints state after up-public]

title: The Ghidra workflow cannot run: ROOT is one directory short and its scripts are missing
description:
tools/ghidra/ghidra-import.sh and ghidra-decompile.sh are unusable as written.

1. ROOT RESOLVES ONE DIRECTORY SHORT. Both compute ROOT as dirname($BASH_SOURCE)/.. which from tools/ghidra/ is tools/, not the repo root. So they look for tools/ghidra/unpacked_mine.bin, tools/ghidra/proj and tools/ghidra/scripts. tools/mips16-xrefs.py resolves the same image to the REPO ROOT ghidra/unpacked_mine.bin, so the two tools disagree about where it lives. The scripts were moved from scripts/ to tools/ (mips16-xrefs.py's own usage text still says 'scripts/mips16-xrefs.py') and the path was not updated with them.

2. THE GHIDRA SCRIPTS ARE NOT IN THE TREE. Both reference DigiboxDump.java (postScript) and DigiboxSetup.java (preScript) under $ROOT/ghidra/scripts. Neither file exists anywhere in the repository -- find . -name 'DigiboxDump.java' returns nothing. So even with ROOT fixed, the import and decompile would fail.

3. ctl.sh HAS NO GHIDRA VERB. ghidra-decompile.sh tells the user to 'run ./ctl.sh ghidra:import first'; grep -c ghidra ctl.sh is 0.

Ghidra itself IS installed (/opt/ghidra, /opt/ghidra_12.1.3_PUBLIC) and Java 21 is present, so the only things missing are the paths and the two Java scripts.

WORKAROUND IN PLACE: tools/disasm.sh renders MIPS16 with mips-linux-gnu-objdump (binutils-mips-linux-gnu, installed 2026-09-21). It is enough to read code and it found the 0xC1 record format. What it does NOT give is Ghidra's decompiler output, which turns a page of MIPS16 into C and is the reason the workflow was built.

NOTE ctl.sh IS GOVERNED (scripts/conformance/rule-guard.sh PROTECTED), so adding the verb needs ./ctl.sh authorise-rules first.
close_reason:
FIXED AND PROVEN 2026-09-22. All three faults in the report, plus two more of the same kind found next door.

1. ROOT: both scripts computed dirname(BASH_SOURCE)/.. from tools/ghidra/, giving tools/. Now /../..
   with a comment saying why, since the symptom was every path silently resolving inside tools/.
2. THE JAVA SCRIPTS NOW EXIST, in tools/ghidra/scripts/ -- NOT ghidra/scripts/, because /ghidra/ is
   gitignored (.gitignore:43) and a committed script cannot live there.
   - DigiboxSetup.java maps FLASH_U202.bin at 0x9FC00000 beside the application image (without it
     every pool word and string is an unresolved pointer) and seeds the 28 proved MIPS16 entry
     points by setting ISA_MODE=1 and disassembling. Seeds rather than a blanket ISA_MODE, because
     blanketing decodes every MIPS32 function into plausible nonsense.
   - DigiboxDump.java decompiles addresses to C, fenced with ==== so the shell wrapper can find the
     output among Ghidra's chatter.
3. ctl.sh HAS THE VERBS: ghidra:import and ghidra:decompile (authorised via ./ctl.sh authorise-rules,
   since ctl.sh is governed).

ALSO FIXED, same class of bug -- a path that did not move with the file:
   tools/opentv-natives.py resolved the flash to frontend/public/FLASH_U202.bin, the PREDECESSOR's
   layout, which this repo has never had; it died in the import on every invocation. Same stale
   default in tools/ocode-disasm.py. Both now firmware/FLASH_U202.bin, and the usage text in all
   three tools still said scripts/ after the move to tools/.

PROVEN, not assumed:
   ./ctl.sh ghidra:import -> 'mapped FLASH_U202.bin (2097152 bytes) at 9fc00000' and 'seeded 28
   MIPS16 entry points', exit 0.
   ./ctl.sh ghidra:decompile 0x800A4B60 -> FUN_800a4a90 in C, and it immediately shows the grid's
   outer gate that hand-reading MIPS16 had not reached:
       local_44 = (*DAT_800a4c84)(iVar1);
       if ((local_44 == 4) || ((local_44 == 2 && (... != 0)))) { ...the whole enumeration... }
   local_44 is the transport health code (state 7 -> 4, state 4/5 -> 2).

NOTE Ghidra CANNOT decompile the o-code the EPG screens are written in -- interpreted bytecode, no
processor module. For that the tool is tools/ocode-disasm.py plus the native-shim census.

title: [TASK-7.10] Establish how many services the grid is actually iterating, live and in RAM
description:
Establish how many services the grid is actually iterating, LIVE and in RAM.

THE DISCREPANCY: docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md has the box counting TWELVE channels
(DS+0x02E20C = 12) and holding "all twelve services" in its 18-byte records, measured 16 Sep. The
demo schedule (listings/default.json) names SIX. So the line-up the restored snapshot carries and
the line-up the transmitter announces may disagree, and a grid iterating twelve entries against a
store that knows six is a plausible way to draw a header and no rows.

WHY THIS RUNS BEFORE ANY DISASSEMBLY: it is one read-watch, it is decisive either way, and the
instrument already exists -- internal/multiplex/grid_firmware_test.go reaches the grid in six
seconds and proves which screen it is on.

NOTE THE RECORD'S ADDRESSES DO NOT APPLY. gort-qxl.1 establishes that DS+0x02E20C's reads at
0x9FC75F7B / 0x9FC762FD / 0x9FC77D41 execute ZERO times during the grid draw: the application runs
decompressed in RAM (region 80______) and those are flash addresses. So this task must find the
count's LIVE address rather than reuse the recorded one -- a read-watch over RAM while the grid
draws, looking for a word holding the service count.

approach: extend grid_firmware_test.go with a read-watch; report the live count beside
len(guide.On(day).Services); a disagreement is the finding and so is agreement.
spec: plan/phase-7-unsolved-screens.md
-> /go-engineer
[TC-7.7]
notes:
SCOPE CLARIFIED after owner challenge 2026-09-21 ('if that's the old inject flash/memory shit...'). It is NOT an injection. It is a READ-WATCH: it observes a word the guest already maintains while the grid draws and compares it with the service count the transmitter announced. Nothing is poked, patched or written.

It is nonetheless DEMOTED to P3, because the owner's direction makes gort-0ly the headline: if the Sky menu gates are answered from the broadcast rather than by patching flash 0x72FA1 and RAM 0x80054F84, the line-up the box holds may change anyway and this measurement would then be taken against a machine in a different state. It survives as Q6 of that idea -- 'does the twelve-versus-six discrepancy dissolve once the gates are answered properly' -- and is worth keeping because it is cheap, decisive either way, and the instrument already exists.
close_reason:
ANSWERED: SIX, and it matches the broadcast exactly. 2026-09-22.

Measured live and in RAM, which is what this task asked for. The box's own 18-byte service records, located by content rather than by address (service id at +4, channel number at +10, both values the fixture chose) with the 18-byte stride taken from the commonest gap rather than assumed:

    802B5340 service 100 channel 101 Sky One       802B5376 service 103 channel 301 Sky Movies
    802B5352 service 101 channel 501 Sky News      802B5388 service 104 channel 251 Sky Travel
    802B5364 service 102 channel 401 Sky Sports 1  802B539A service 105 channel 121 Sky Soap

One record per announced service. THE RESTORED LINE-UP AND THE BROADCAST LINE-UP DO NOT DISAGREE, so the hypothesis this task was filed on -- that a grid iterating twelve entries against a store of six would draw a header and no rows -- is dead. 'The box counts twelve channels' is the browser oracle's number in the oracle's own address space and does not describe this port.

AND THE GRID DOES NOT ITERATE THEM ANYWAY: a read watch over those records during the draw logged zero reads in 488,551, and no read anywhere in DRAM returned 501, 401 or 301. It is not filtering our channels out; it never has them. So the count was never the gate -- consistent with the oracle, whose grid knew twelve channels and drew none either.

INSTRUMENT: internal/multiplex/firmwaretests/lineupcount_firmware_test.go. It fails unless it finds every announced service, so its count is a reading rather than a number about nothing.

Where the grid DOES get its list is now the whole of gort-qxl.1, retitled around the walked tables at 0x8045D000 and 0x80494000 and the o-code at 0x9FC5D000.

title: Remove the stale listings.json mount artefact and the unused web/data leftovers
description:
Two pieces of dead weight found by the phase 6 security audit. Neither is a vulnerability; both are tidy-ups that remove things that look load-bearing and are not.

1. `listings.json/` at the repo root is an EMPTY ROOT-OWNED DIRECTORY left behind by the old bind mount `./listings.json:/listings/listings.json`, which Docker created when the path did not exist. The mount changed to `./listings:/listings` -- the change is recorded in .conformance-authorised row 91. Git cannot see it because it is empty, so it does not show in git status and will sit there indefinitely. Remove with `sudo rmdir listings.json` (root-owned, so it needs sudo).

2. `web/data/listings.json` and `web/data/sky-huffman.js` are tracked, have no Go consumer, and are NOT served: internal/app/app.go:48-57 is an explicit route map with an exact-path check, so anything under web/data/ returns 404 (verified live -- curl for /listings, /listings/default.json and /dictionaries/skyuk.dict on the public host all returned 404). They are oracle-era leftovers.

Do item 2 together with gort-a40, which removes web/data/skyuk.dict from the same directory for licence reasons -- one commit, one directory, rather than two passes over the same files.

title: Unbounded reads and quadratic re-encoding from operator listings, on the instruction loop
description:
Operator listings do unbounded and quadratic work ON THE INSTRUCTION LOOP. Found by the phase 6 security audit; NOT TIMED, so treat the magnitude as unmeasured.

Three places, all reached from the loop rather than from a goroutine (which is correct per the no-goroutine rule -- the cost is the point, not the threading):
1. stampOf (internal/multiplex/listings.go:216-254) READS AND SHA-256 HASHES EVERY *.json in the schedule directory on each line-up wave (multiplex.go:249, roughly every 60M instructions). It is called on the carousel's own cadence, so it runs many times per real edit -- by design, but the cost scales with the directory.
2. LoadListings (listings.go:273) has NO SIZE CAP. os.ReadFile on whatever the operator put there.
3. records() (multiplex.go:424-454) RE-ENCODES the growing quarter once per programme -- it appends a candidate and calls TitleSection to ask whether it still fits. That is quadratic in programmes per channel, with a Huffman encode inside each pass.

This interacts with the 15M instr/s NFR (gort-4sx.29, currently ~3.2M/s): work on the loop is exactly what that task is trying to claw back. Anyone touching either should read both.

TRUST BOUNDARY: operator-supplied files on a read-only production mount. Not internet-reachable. Availability/performance only.

FIX: stat the file size before reading and refuse above a few MB; cap programmes per channel in validate(); consider hashing size+mtime first and only reading when those move. MEASURE FIRST -- record an instructions-per-second figure with a large schedule directory before and after, because no such figure exists in the repo today and a fix with no measurement is how the predecessor's performance work went wrong.

title: Use canonical hex formatting in firmware trace instruments
description: Reconciliation architecture finding: cmd/firmwaretrace/main.go and tasks.go emit guest addresses with raw %08X while pc_hits.go emits %#x, violating CLAUDE.md hexfmt convention and risking case/width mismatches. Migrate these trace/address consumers to internal/platform/hexfmt in one change and remove duplicate formatting; preserve the comparator wire format deliberately. Agent: /go-engineer. Test with addressed PC hit containing A-F and compare oracle artifact parsing. Covers TC-3a.7.
close_reason: Firmware trace, task census and PC-hit diagnostics now format through hexfmt; wire adapter preserves existing uppercase no-prefix comparator fields. Unit test checks A-F address and widths; fresh v2 restored 650M→680M SI trace passed unchanged comparator over six samples, nine guest PCs, four match units; race tests/lint/replay gate pass.

title: Audit the 55 %x/%X uses in test files for address-casing drift
description:
CARRIED FROM PHASE 1, stated by p1-core rather than silently skipped, and deliberately NOT swept at shutdown.

PRODUCT CODE IS CLEAN. Commit c7766ef routed every address a human sees through hexfmt (Addr/Range/Byte), and TestEveryAddressShownToAHumanIsCanonical now guards the CLASS rather than a list -- it drives every refusal the bus package can produce plus the panic, checks every 0x-prefixed run for upper case AND canonical width, and returns a HARNESS FAILURE when a message contains no address at all, since a message with nothing to check cannot vouch for anything. A refusal added in phase 2 is covered the moment it is exercised. Verified by the lead: no non-hexfmt address formatting remains anywhere in internal/ or cmd/ outside tests.

WHAT IS LEFT: 55 uses of %x / %X across the module's TEST files. Some are legitimately not addresses (byte diffs, expected values, hash literals). p1-core declined to sweep them at the end of a long session on the grounds that it was more likely to introduce noise than remove risk, and -- the honest part -- did NOT claim they are all fine, because it had not read all 55.

WHY IT IS A REAL TASK RATHER THAN A SWEEP: each site needs a judgement about whether the value is an ADDRESS (canonical hexfmt form, because a reader will grep docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md for it), a LENGTH (decimal -- padding a length to eight hex digits makes it read as an address, and hexfmt has no length form because nobody greps the record for a length), or an opaque value like a hash (whatever the surrounding assertion needs). That distinction is exactly what p1-core applied when it left two sites alone and made them decimal instead.

WHY IT MATTERS AT ALL, given they are only tests: a test that PRINTS a lower-case address sends the reader of a failure to the wrong place in the record -- the same cost as the product-code defect, just one step further from the machine. It is low priority because a wrong pointer in a diagnostic costs minutes, not a wrong answer.

WORTH FRESH EYES rather than the author's. p1-core said so itself.

source: c7766ef, 071c7d2; the hexfmt rationale in CLAUDE.md
agent: /go-engineer
close_reason: Audited test-file hex formatting: address operands in bus/memory diagnostics now use canonical hexfmt.Addr; lengths and device offsets use decimal; firmware reset words use hexfmt.Word and offset uses hexfmt.Byte. Remaining hex operands are data words, byte/half values, or opaque state hashes. Race tests and lint pass.

title: Re-point three comments at the retired boot gate's successor record
description:
tools/check-digibox-boot.mjs was retired in commit 2c8779c; what it measured now lives in docs/reference/oracle-boot-gate.md and the one check that needed no browser is a Go test in internal/oracle. Three comments still cite the dead tool -- and cite it at scripts/check-digibox-boot.mjs, a path it did not occupy in this repository, which is its own evidence of how long it had gone unmaintained:

- reference/digibox-boot.html:740  (the warm/cold ceiling note -- 'measured by ..., which has clicked Max on every run')
- reference/digibox-boot.html:5189 (the TASK20 scheduling wait)
- docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md:4645 (the readiness readout note)

Point them at docs/reference/oracle-boot-gate.md. Do NOT delete the surrounding text: each comment records a MEASURED fact (the warm/cold instruction ceilings, what the gate waited on) and those facts outlived the tool. Only the citation is stale.

OWNERSHIP: p1-core -- reference/digibox-boot.html and docs/reference/ are its files. p1-platform found these while retiring the tool and deliberately did not make a cross-boundary edit, which is why this is an issue rather than a silent fix.

Low priority: a wrong pointer in a comment costs a reader five minutes, not a wrong answer. Fold it into any commit that already touches those files rather than making a commit of its own.

agent: /go-engineer
close_reason: Three stale citations re-pointed at docs/reference/oracle-boot-gate.md (reference/digibox-boot.html:740 and :5211, docs/reference/digibox-emulation.md:4645). Only the citations changed: each comment records a measured fact that outlived the tool - the 31s warm / 96s cold ceilings at 400,000 instructions per frame, and that the gate waited for TASK20 to stop being scheduled because a key pressed during the bank-1 CRC is dropped on the CSI link - and deleting the surrounding text would have thrown away the measurement to fix the footnote. The only remaining mentions of the retired tool are in the successor record itself, which is where they belong. go test -race clean.

title: Add govulncheck to CI, pinned to a version that builds under Go 1.22
description:
Deliberately left out of TASK-1.4. ADR 0001 records that govulncheck still matters precisely BECAUSE the dependency set is empty: standard-library CVEs are now the only category this project can have, so the vulnerability surface is entirely stdlib and entirely invisible without this step.

It was omitted rather than guessed because installing it needs a version that builds under Go 1.22 (the host ceiling -- no fetchable newer toolchain), and shipping a CI step whose install command was guessed at is how a gate arrives broken or, worse, silently skipped. That was the right call.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THE TASK, and it is worth escalating rather than burying: govulncheck reports 29 vulnerabilities THIS TREE ACTUALLY CALLS, all in the standard library, and 25 of them are fixed only in Go 1.23 or later. ADR 0001 records that no external dependencies makes the stdlib the entire supply-chain surface; what it did not anticipate is that the surface is EOL and unpatchable here. Four of the 29 are fixable within the 1.22 line (1.22.3/1.22.4/1.22.11/1.22.12); the remaining 25 need a toolchain this host cannot fetch. THE REAL FIX IS A NEWER GO, and this gate is a way of living with that honestly rather than a substitute for it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GATE'S SHAPE: a plain `govulncheck ./...` step would be red on every run for ever, with nothing any committer could do about it. That is not strictness; it is a gate people stop reading — the same decoration failure as a permanently green one, arrived at from the other side. So the gate asks the answerable question: is there anything NEW? Anything not in the committed baseline fails. A baseline entry no longer reported is PRINTED but does not fail, because the exact set varies with the 1.22.x patch level and failing on it would be unactionable — the same reasoning that scoped the pre-commit hook to the packages being committed.

THE PIN WAS WRONG ON FIRST ATTEMPT AND I CAUGHT IT BY TESTING: the issue title says "pinned to a version that builds under Go 1.22", and the locally installed govulncheck v1.3.0 reports `Go: go1.22.2`, which looks like confirmation. It is not — that field is the toolchain it ANALYSES with, not the one that built it. `go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@v1.3.0` fails outright: `golang.org/x/vuln@v1.3.0 requires go >= 1.25.0`. Checked the go directive of each candidate and pinned v1.1.4, the newest whose directive is `go >= 1.22.0`. Verified it installs and runs under Go 1.22 locally AND on the CI runner, and that it produces an identical 29-id finding set to v1.3.0, so the baseline is scanner-independent in practice.

PROVED RED THEN GREEN ON THE RUNNER, not merely locally. A scratch branch with one accepted id removed: run 35128961244 FAILED the vulnerabilities job, reporting `25 called, 28 accepted, 1 new` and naming GO-2026-6090 with its advisory URL. Restoring the id gave run 35129103117, GREEN (`25 called, 29 accepted, 0 new`). That exercised the entire path on the runner — installing the pinned scanner under Go 1.22, jq, the scan, the JSON extraction and the comparison. The throwaway PR (#2, draft, DO NOT MERGE) is closed with an explanatory comment, the branch is deleted from origin and locally, the worktree is removed, and `git ls-remote` confirms origin/master is still at f54e9bf.

THE RUNNER VINDICATED THE BASELINE DESIGN BY ACCIDENT, which is the most useful thing the proof produced: it reported 25 called against our 29, because its Go is a newer 1.22.x than this machine's 1.22.2. Generating the baseline from the OLDEST toolchain in use makes it a superset, so a newer patch level reports a subset, produces nothing new, and stays green without anyone pinning patch versions to keep it that way. Had "no longer reported" been a failure, CI would have been red from its very first run for a reason no committer could act on.

FOUR MORE FAILURE PATHS WATCHED LOCALLY, through a `--report` seam that feeds the gate a captured scan (an input override, not a bypass — the comparison is identical either way, and it exists so the gate can be tested without a 30-second scan each time): a new vulnerability -> RED naming it; a baseline that accepts nothing -> RED as a harness failure; an empty report -> RED, because an empty report is not a clean tree; and a report with only unreachable findings -> GREEN, which is correct since nothing is called.

ONE TRAP GUARDED IN A COMMENT because it would silently disarm the gate: with `-format json`, govulncheck EXITS 0 even when it finds vulnerabilities — the exit-3 convention is text-format only. Anyone "simplifying" this to trust the scanner's exit status would produce a gate that always passes. The verdict comes from the comparison; a non-zero status there means the scan itself failed.

Only symbol-level (called) findings are gated. Imported-but-not-called vulnerabilities — 62 of them — are not listed and not gated, because our code has no path to them.
